115. The ITA considers the nominee and nominator indistinctly. $^{20}$ There are requirements for international companies, domestic companies and foreign companies which are resident for tax purposes in the Cook Islands to furnish an annual return of income in the prescribed form, including the full names and addresses of shareholders and, if a shareholder holds their shares as a nominee, trustee or the shareholder is otherwise not the beneficial owner, the company must also provide the full name and address of the beneficial owners of the shares $^{21}$ (Income Tax Act, s. 8, company tax return RM 6). There are no further instructions in the form on how to comply with this. While completing the income tax return may cause the company to provide information on a nominator in respect of a shareholder that is known by the company to be a nominee, there is nothing in the Income Tax Act or other laws of the Cook Islands that would require a nominee to disclose their status as nominee to the company or to provide information on the nominator to the company. Availability of complete information with the RMD on nominee arrangements is therefore not ensured.

116. In summary, some information may be available for each type of company on nominees and their nominators through requirements in the Companies Act, the FTRA and tax law. However, there are no requirements that would comprehensively require nominees to disclose their status to a Cook Islands company and provide information to the company on their nominator, so it is not ensured that the information available will be complete. The Cook Islands is recommended to ensure that ownership and identity information is available in respect of nominee shareholdings.

117. As described in the 2015 Report, nominee arrangements are very rare for domestic companies, many of which are small and owned by a husband and wife, and this remains the case. In contrast, nominee arrangements are common in limited liability companies and international companies (see paragraphs 50 and 60).
Availability of legal ownership information in EOIR practice

118. During the review period, the Cook Islands received seven requests for legal ownership information on international companies. The answers were provided on time and the partners were satisfied with the information.
Availability of beneficial ownership information

119. The standard was strengthened in 2016 to require that beneficial ownership information be available on companies. Beneficial ownership information in the Cook Islands is collected primarily through the AML framework. Because this source of information would not necessarily capture all domestic companies, in 2017 the Cook Islands introduced an additional mechanism with the Companies Act requiring companies to obtain and maintain some beneficial ownership information, although the definition at that time did not meet the standard. The definition was amended towards the end of the current review period and both the former and current definitions are analysed further below.

$^{20}$ ITA, s. 3(3): “Where a nominee of any person holds any shares, nominal capital, paid-up capital or voting power in a company, or has by any other means whatsoever any power of control of a company, or is entitled to a share of profits distributed by a company then, for the purposes of this section, those shares or that capital or that voting power or that power of control or that title to profits as the case may be, shall be deemed to be held by that person, and in every such case that person and the nominee or nominees of that person shall be deemed to be one person.”

$^{21}$ This obligation does not amount to identifying the beneficial owners of the company, as the obligation applies to some shares only and no definition is provided of beneficial owner is this context.

text: Company law requirements

121. Prior to 4 December 2024, domestic companies were required to obtain and maintain sufficient information to identify the beneficial owner of each share issued by the company. Companies were not generally required to file this information with the Registrar, they were only required to disclose this information if required to do so in a written notice issued by the Registrar (CA 2017, s. 52(2)). While the Companies Act 2017 required all companies to reregister on a new online system by a deadline ultimately extended to 31 March 2022, this process did not require any information on beneficial owners to be added to the system.
122. Formerly, section 52(3) of the Companies Act defined a beneficial owner as:
the person who ultimately owns or controls the share

123. This definition and related obligation departed from the standard. The Cook Islands legislation did not require domestic companies to keep information about their beneficial ownership but about the beneficial ownership of each share.

124. While the definition of beneficial owner referred to “person”, it was not clear if that meant a natural person or could also be a legal person. There was also no default position where an individual in a senior managerial position would be identified. Individuals having either ultimate ownership or control of the share appeared to be covered; however, persons having ultimate control of the company through means other than ownership would not be identified. It was also not clear whether “ultimately” would be interpreted as meaning any person who controls the share acting directly or indirectly, or acting individually or jointly. The beneficial ownership information was therefore not required to be maintained in line with the standard under the company law requirements. $^{24}$

125. Most importantly, the requirement was not to obtain and maintain information on the identity of the beneficial owners, it was to obtain and maintain sufficient information to identify the beneficial owners. This falls short of actually identifying the beneficial owners and, even if there might be sufficient information assembled under which it could be done if required, the adequacy of the assembled information is not tested by doing so. Furthermore, there was no specification of identity information on the beneficial owners that should be covered by this – such as name, address, date of birth, etc.

126. The Companies Act was amended with effect from 4 December 2024, so that the requirement is now to obtain and maintain sufficient information to identify the beneficial owners of the company. While the amendment improved the definition of beneficial owners as further discussed below, it did not remove the concern over only requiring sufficient information to identify the beneficial owners instead of clearly requiring that there is a process carried out to actually identify them. It also remains the case that there is no specification of the identity information on the beneficial owners that should be available (for example, name, address, date of birth, other details). These gaps are discussed further at paragraph 136).

127. The definition of beneficial owner was also amended to have the same meaning as “ultimate principal” provided by the FTRA. At the same time, the definition of ultimate principal in the FTRA was amended so that beneficial owner (ultimate principal) now means, for both the Companies Act and the FTRA:
(1) ...the 1 or more natural persons -
(a) who exercise ultimate effective control over a legal person or legal arrangement...

(2) In this section, exercise ultimate effective control includes where ownership or control is exercised through a chain of ownership or by any means of control other than direct control; and as further provided in regulations.
128. Regulation 6 of the FTRA regulations was also amended to elaborate on the meaning of “ultimate principal” in the Act. The part relevant to ultimate principals of legal persons is as follows:
(1) This regulation sets out further detail for identifying ultimate principals who exercise ultimate effective control over a legal person or legal arrangement.
(2) (a) the natural persons who
(i) ultimately hold directly or indirectly, jointly or otherwise, 25% or more of the shares in the capital or voting rights of the legal person; or
(ii) are jointly and severally liable for the liabilities, regardless of their percentage of the capital or voting rights in the legal person

(b) if, under subclause (1)(a), no natural person is identified or there are doubts about whether the natural persons identified are ultimate principals, the natural persons who control the legal person by any other means, de facto or de jure
(c) if no natural person is identified under subclause (1)(a) or (b), the natural persons who hold the position of senior managing official.

$^{24}$ No ordinance (secondary legislation/by-laws), guidance or case law was provided that would have explained the definition of beneficial owner as provided under the company law applicable prior to 4 December 2024.

(3) A natural person who meets 1 or more of the specified conditions under subclause (2) is deemed to be an ultimate principal unless that person operates solely in the capacity of a professional advisor or professional manager.

(4) If no natural person meets any of the specified conditions under subclause (2) and the trustees of a trust meet one or more of those specified conditions, the trustees of the trust are deemed to be the ultimate principals unless they are exercising ultimate effective control over the activities of the trust solely in the capacity of a professional adviser, professional manager or trustee company.
(5) If no natural person is identified as an ultimate principal under subclauses (2) to (4), any senior managing official is deemed to be the ultimate principal.

129. These amendments have resolved most of the previous deficiencies in the definition of beneficial owner in the Companies Act by ensuring that the relevant persons to be identified are natural persons, the relevant control is over the company and not each share, that control may be direct or indirect, acting jointly with other persons, and that a senior managing official is identified in the event that no other beneficial owners are identified.

130. Some observations may be made on the new definition and cascading approach to identify beneficial owners. Firstly, cross-reference errors appear to have been made in clause (2), by referring to subclause (1)(a) and again subclauses (1)(a) and (b) when no subclauses of clause (1) exist. It is relatively clear that the intention was to refer to subclauses (2)(a) and (b). The relevant Cook Islands' supervisory authority for the FTRA confirms that this was the intention and expects this to be enforceable despite the error.
131. Secondly, clause (2) closely follows the standard and would meet the standard. However, it is subject to clauses (3) to (5) which must also be examined to assess the full outcome.

132. Clause (3) excludes a person who is operating solely in the capacity of professional advisor. Professional advisor is defined in the regulations and includes a lawyer, an accountant or a financial advisor acting in a professional capacity. Clause (3) also excludes professional managers, and these are defined to include liquidators, receivers and officers of the FSC exercising their statutory functions. While these exclusions could be appropriate in relation to persons who would otherwise be in scope under subclauses (2)(a) and (b), the exclusion would not always be appropriate in the event that it became necessary to apply the default mechanism of subclause (2)(c) – the identification of a senior managing official. It is noted that clause (5) reintroduces the requirement to identify senior managing officials if no natural person has been identified under clauses (2) to (4), which should bring back into scope any relevant professional advisor or professional manager that meets the description of being a senior managing official when no other ultimate principals have been identified. It remains that the interplay of the clauses is complex and may lead to difficulties in implementation.

133. If no natural person is identified by clause (2), clause (4) will deem the trustees of a trust to be ultimate principals if they meet any of the conditions in clause (2). It goes on to then exclude a trustee of a trust from being an ultimate principal if they are a professional advisor, professional manager or trustee company. Again, these exclusions could be appropriate in relation to persons otherwise in scope under subclauses (2)(a) and (b), however the exclusion would not always be appropriate in the event that it became necessary to apply the default mechanism of subclause (2)(c) – the identification of a senior managing official. Furthermore, under the client structures and arrangements under which trustee companies in the Cook Islands commonly provide services, it seems very unlikely that no other persons would have been identified as ultimate principals by reason of their roles in relation to the trust or as natural persons to whom the professional advisor, professional manager or trustee company is in substance providing their services. The reference to a trustee company potentially needing the benefit of the exclusion in clause (4) adds some doubt over the intention or operation of the clause, as such entities should never be identified as ultimate principals under the standard as they are not natural persons.

134. No guidance has been issued by the authorities on the operation of these clauses in the new definition for either the Companies Act or the FTRA. A representative of a trustee company indicated that it was not aware of the purpose of clauses (3) and (4) in the new definition and in practice it did not apply these to modify the operation of clause (2). According to the FSC, almost all trustee company business is referred through professional intermediaries and typically there will be a variety of advisors (lawyers, investment advisors, etc.) that may have some role in the structure. The trustee companies are required to identify and verify these intermediaries, however the purpose of clauses (3) and (4) is to ensure that they do not stop at that point and must continue further to the client individual(s) ultimately behind the structure. If they can only identify the professional intermediaries or advisors in their CDD processes (i.e. not the client that is providing the instructions or the assets to the structure) then the FSC expects the reporting institution not to proceed at all with the relationship.

135. While the definition of beneficial owner (ultimate principal) now applicable under the Companies Act and the FTRA may be interpreted with a meaning that is in line with the standard, there is some complexity to the exclusions for professional advisors and managers and it would benefit from guidance from the authorities to ensure these do not cause the definition to depart from the standard in practice. The Cook Islands should clarify in guidance the operation of the definition of beneficial owner in relation to professional advisors and managers (see Annex 1).

136. While there is an obligation on a domestic company to obtain and maintain beneficial ownership information, there are several deficiencies that could result in a failure to have available all information that would meet the standard. As mentioned at paragraphs 125 and 126, previous deficiencies around completing the process of identifying the beneficial owners and the lack of specification of the identity details that need to be obtained remain the case and were not resolved by the amendment in December 2024. The Companies Act also does not provide for any mechanism under which the company might compel the provision of information from shareholders or beneficial owners. It does not impose any onus on a shareholder or a beneficial owner to disclose information to the company or to inform the company of any changes. No sanctions are envisaged in case a shareholder or beneficial owner refuses to co-operate with the company. The legal framework therefore lacks mechanisms under which domestic companies can obtain and update beneficial ownership information. Furthermore, even if a company has the ability to comply, no timeframes have been specified within which they must do so. No timeframe was originally given under which companies could transition to compliance under the original requirements introduced in 2017. The amendments effective from 4 December 2024 also did not specify any timeframe within which companies would be required to obtain and maintain any new information to comply with the amended requirements. In this context, the only sanction available if a company fails to comply is an offence provision requiring conviction by the court (see paragraph 151). This has never been tested, and doubts arise over whether a court would sanction a failure when what would constitute a failure (in terms of missing identity information) has not been specified and in any case no deadline for compliance has been provided. In summary, there is an absence of mechanisms under which domestic companies can obtain and update beneficial ownership information and even if it is feasible for a company to do so, a failure to comply may not be enforceable. The deficiency is not mitigated by the AML framework as domestic companies are not required to engage an AML-obliged person in all cases (see paragraph 140). The Cook Islands is recommended to ensure that adequate, accurate and up-to-date beneficial ownership information is available for domestic companies in line with the standard.

137. No information or guidance has been issued by the Registrar of Companies to inform companies of the new requirements or to provide any transitional period under which they may be permitted to come into compliance. These circumstances and the lack of any monitoring and verification activities by the Registrar of Companies in practice (see paragraph 97), lead to significant doubts on the extent to which domestic companies have implemented the original or revised beneficial ownership information requirements, if at all. The Cook Islands is recommended to implement effective oversight and enforcement measures to ensure the availability of beneficial ownership information for domestic companies.

Anti-money laundering law requirements

138. Registration of international companies and limited liability companies must be conducted through a licensed trustee company in the Cook Islands, $^{25}$ each of which are reporting institutions under the AML framework (see paragraph 77). The trustee company is required to conduct CDD procedures to identify and verify the beneficial owners (FTRA 2017, ss. 25 to 30) before establishing the relationship (prior to registration of the prospective client entity). Each international company and limited liability company must continue to have an ongoing relationship with a trustee company. Thus, information on beneficial ownership of these companies is required to be kept with the licensed trustee companies.

139. International companies and limited liability companies will rarely if ever have a bank account with the domestic banks. These entities sometimes have a bank account with the international bank operating in the Cook Islands. Banks are therefore at best a secondary source for beneficial ownership information on these entities.

140. For domestic companies, beneficial ownership under the AML framework will be available only if they have an ongoing relationship with an AML-obliged person, for instance a bank. There is no legal obligation that requires or would cause a domestic company to have an ongoing relationship with an AML-obliged person, which means that the AML framework does not provide for a complete source of information on beneficial ownership of domestic companies. The Cook Islands understands that domestic companies would commonly have a bank account, although this is not assured, nor is it assured that such bank accounts would be held with a Cook Islands bank. To date, there has been no requirement to obtain beneficial ownership information on domestic companies for EOI purposes, so there is no experience in practice.
141. Pursuant to FTRA 2017, when dealing with a customer that is not a natural person, reporting institutions are required to do the following:
\- identify and verify any “ultimate principal” of the customer
• verify the status of the customer
\- obtain sufficient information to understand the customer's business and its ownership and control structure and
\- obtain information concerning the person(s) by whom, and the method by which, binding obligations may be imposed on the customer $^{26}$ (FTRA 2017, s. 25).

142. The types, kinds or categories of identity information to be obtained or verified for meeting the requirements above and any additional due diligence requirements may be prescribed in Regulations, and the Cook Islands has done so. In the case of a natural person, the identifying information to be obtained includes the full name, residential address, date and place of birth, nationality and an official personal identification number or other unique identifier in a valid official document. In the case of legal persons and legal arrangements, various identification information is also prescribed, and it includes the same identification requirements mentioned for natural persons that are ultimate principals and other natural persons acting on behalf of the legal person or legal arrangement. The primary Act requires, and the
$^{25}$ Section 9 of the International Companies Act, and section 5 of the Limited Liability Companies Act.

$^{26}$ This includes the memorandum and articles of association for a company, the partnership agreement, trust deed and foundation rules in the case of partnerships, trusts and foundations respectively. It can also include information that explains the management and control structure of the legal person. It can include mergers and acquisition, organisational chart, internal policies, etc.

Regulations reiterate, that verification of identity and information to be based on documents, data or information issued by a reliable and independent source.

143. A reporting institution that is unable to meet the customer due diligence requirements of the FTRA must terminate the relationship and consider whether to submit a suspicious activity report to the FSC. If the reporting institution reasonably believes that undertaking the customer due diligence or terminating the relationship would tip off the customer, it must submit a suspicious activity report within 24 hours.

144. Reporting institutions are required to maintain up-to-date and current CDD information on their clients (FTRA 2017, s. 32). The retention period is six years from the end of the relationship or the one-off transaction (FTRA 2017, s. 44). A reporting institution must carry out ongoing and effective monitoring of any ongoing business relationship, including the review of information held for the purpose of CDD to ensure that it is up to date and appropriate. The reporting institution must make sure that the extent and frequency of the monitoring appropriately reflect: (i) the type of CDD conducted when the ongoing business relationship with the customer was established, and (ii) the customer's level of risk (FTRA 2017, s. 32(2)(3)). Practice Guidelines issued by the FSC also explain that the reporting institution should take note of any changes in the nature of the relationship with the customer, such as changes in activities, turnover or transactions and when significant, reassess the customer's risk profile and the basis of the ongoing relationship.

145. There is no specified frequency for updating CDD. Practice Guidelines issued by the FSC advise that CDD information must be reviewed periodically, and monitoring frequencies are “suggested” as at least every three years for standard risk customers and annually for high-risk customers. In practice, only some reporting institutions follow this suggestion with a specified default cycle time and some others instead only apply a trigger-based system, or their system is trigger based for some clients. These trigger-based approaches have been considered by the FSC as acceptable under its Guidelines. In the case of trustee companies, CDD is in practice is always updated at least annually when preparing the annual returns required to be filed for international companies and limited liability companies. However, representatives of the domestic banks stated that they classify clients in terms of risk as high, medium or low. High risk clients, a category that includes every client with indications of foreign residence, are reviewed on a cycle of 6 to 12 months. Medium and low risk client reviews are trigger based, with re-evaluation triggered by any change in information held on the client that may affect their risk rating. The international bank stated that it has no cycle time for re-assessment of clients based on their risk classification, with re-assessment based on triggers similar to those applied by domestic banks but applied for all clients. An exception to this is for politically exposed persons who are subject to enhanced ongoing monitoring and must be reviewed annually.

146. The definition of “ultimate principal” was amended towards the end of the review period (see paragraph 127), so it is necessary to examine both the previous and the current definitions. Prior to 4 December 2024, the definition of “ultimate principal” was defined as (FTRA 2017, s. 8):
one or more natural persons who ultimately own or effectively control the customer, or on whose behalf a transaction or activity is being conducted and includes:

(i) in the case of a legal person, other than a company whose securities are listed on a recognised stock exchange, any natural person who ultimately owns or effectively controls (whether through direct or indirect ownership or control, including through bear share holdings) 25% or more of the shares or voting rights in the legal person;
(ii) In the case of any legal person, it includes any natural person who otherwise exercises effective control over the management of the legal person;

147. Section 8 therefore operated to provide the definition of beneficial owner in the Act, including providing a threshold for ownership or control. It also made it clear that ownership or control may be direct or indirect. While the definition contained the principal elements required by the standard, it was not clear that control will include a person acting individually or jointly, although this could have been captured by the term “otherwise”. There was a simultaneous approach to the definition of beneficial owner in the case of a legal person which was in line with the standard.

148. However, the definition did not contemplate the identification of the individuals holding a senior managerial position in cases where a beneficial owner cannot be identified. The Companies Act did not compensate for this absence, as it did not require the names of senior managers to be registered with the Registrar. This allowed the possibility that no beneficial owner would be identified in some cases.

149. The definition of ultimate principal in the FTRA and in regulations made under that law was amended with effect from 4 December 2024. For legal persons, this has been analysed in paragraphs 126 to 133 in relation to the use of this definition in the Companies Act and the same observations apply for its application under the FTRA. Specifically, the definition of ultimate principal and cascading method for their identification now applicable under the FTRA may be interpreted in line with the standard, however it would benefit from guidance from the authorities to ensure correct application in practice. The Cook Islands should clarify in guidance the operation of the definition of ultimate principal in relation to professional advisors and managers (see Annex 1). Additionally, as noted in paragraph 136, the amendments did not specify any timeframe within which reporting institutions would be required to redetermine the ultimate principals of account holders or clients under the amended requirements. In practice though, the change in definition of ultimate principal in the FTRA was less substantial than the change in definition of beneficial owner in the Companies Act, and the FSC states that the amendment did not require any change to their pre-existing practices which were in effect already aligned to the amended definition. Representatives of the reporting institutions concurred with this assessment, noting that it was already their practice to identify senior managing officials.
Conclusion

150. The availability of beneficial ownership information for companies other than domestic companies is dependent on and ensured by the AML framework. However, there is no specified frequency for updating beneficial ownership information under the AML framework. In the case of domestic companies, beneficial ownership information is required to be maintained by the companies themselves. This information source is supported by the AML framework as a potential secondary source of information to the extent that a domestic company has a relationship with an AML obliged person. Some beneficial ownership information may also be available under tax law, although those requirements are not in line with the standard. The Cook Islands is recommended to ensure that adequate, accurate and up-to-date beneficial ownership information is available for all relevant legal entities and arrangements in line with the standard.
Beneficial ownership information – Enforcement measures and oversight

151. If a domestic company fails to obtain and maintain sufficient information to identify the beneficial owner a penalty is applicable to the company and every director, but only if the company fails to provide that information to the Registrar when requested to do so by written notice. In the event of such failure, (i) the company commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding NZD 10 000 (EUR 5 040), and (ii) every director commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding NZD 10 000 (EUR 5 040) or to a term of imprisonment not exceeding 12 months, or both (CA 2017, s. 52).

152. The Registrar of Companies, and the Ministry of Justice of which it is part, is generally responsible for Compliance with the Companies Act. There is no requirement to file beneficial ownership information with the Registrar, and so whether companies are complying with their obligation to obtain and maintain information sufficient to identify their beneficial owners would depend on the Registrar requesting this information or otherwise examining the records held by companies. No routine inspections or audits of any kind were conducted during the review period. No penalty would be applicable in any case if such activities were to be conducted and identify non-compliance. Enforcement would be possible if the Registrar was to formally request these records, however no requests for records relevant to the beneficial ownership subject are known to have been issued during the review period or at any time before or since. The extent to which domestic companies are complying with their obligations under the Companies Act on beneficial owners is therefore unknown.

153. For the AML framework, there are two oversight bodies – the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) and the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU). The FIU was merged with the FSC in 2012. Despite being merged, each body has its own responsibilities and focuses on specific areas. The FSC is responsible for the overall supervision of regulated financial entities and financial services. The FIU's function is to facilitate the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of money laundering, the financing of terrorism and other serious offences (any offence with a term of imprisonment of 12 months or more). To do this, the FIU is empowered under the Financial Intelligence Unit Act 2015 (FIUA 2015) to examine their compliance with the FTRA and the Regulations. The FIU may request information from reporting institutions, conduct on-site examinations and provide reports for this purpose.

154. Penalties upon conviction of an offence under the FTRA are (i) in the case of individuals, a fine not exceeding NZD 250 000 (EUR 126 000), or imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or both; or (ii) in any other case, a fine not exceeding NZD 1 000 000 (EUR 504 000) and other measures such as revocation of licence if the offender is licensed (FTRA 2017, s. 63).

155. Prior to July 2022, every bank and trustee company had at least one onsite inspection each year, (except for 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic when only the three largest trustee companies were inspected). From July 2022, the cycle time remains annual for banks but changed for trustee companies which moved to a two-year inspection cycle. Inspections are primarily onsite and include, among other things, verifying compliance with the FTRA. Compliance with CDD obligations is a key focus. For trustee companies, these are the same inspections as described in paragraphs 105 to 108 that are combined exercises by the FSC to verify compliance by trustee companies with the FTRA, the ICA and the LLCA. As noted in those paragraphs, files on 20-25 clients of a trustee company are selected for review and it can be the case that there are multiple entities in the structure provided for the client. Every entity connected with a client is reviewed and the statistics can be found in the table at paragraph 106.

156. Insofar as banks could be a source of information on beneficial ownership of companies under the AML framework, the FSC's inspections of banks provide assurance over the information they hold. The base minimum file review always includes the CDD requirements related to obtaining and verifying identity information for both legal and beneficial owners of the customer, purpose of relationship, documentation of control and management (corporate documents, trust deeds, letters of wishes, application forms), source of wealth and validation of wealth sources. Between 20 and 25 customers are selected for review, the mix of which will tend to reflect the client base of the bank. The representation of companies and company type in these reviews therefore varies according to the bank's client base. For example, any bank accounts maintained in the Cook Islands for international companies, limited liability companies, international trusts and foundations are concentrated with the international bank, as these generally do not have a relationship with any of the domestic banks. Both legal and beneficial ownership information of a customer is subject to review in these inspections. In terms of the frequency of updating CDD, the FSC reviews found the practices of banks to be as described in paragraph 145 (which it accepted). text: 157. In summary, an appropriate supervisory framework is in place for the AML framework which assures the availability of beneficial ownership information for international companies and limited liability companies. However, the company law framework which is relied upon for the availability of beneficial ownership on domestic companies has had little or no relevant supervision. The AML framework may mitigate this gap, but domestic companies are not required to have a relationship with an AML-obliged person. Tax law may also provide some mitigation, but the monitoring and enforcement of the relevant obligations under tax law also has gaps. The Cook Islands is recommended to implement effective oversight and enforcement measures to ensure the availability of adequate, accurate and up to date beneficial ownership information for domestic companies.
Availability of beneficial ownership information in EOIR practice

158. During the review period, the Cook Islands received seven requests for beneficial ownership information on international companies. Information was provided and the partners were satisfied with the information.
A.1.2 Bearer shares

159. Bearer shares are prohibited under the Companies Act and, in the event that any were to be issued, such shares are a nullity (CA, s. 19). Limited liability companies established under the LLCA do not have their capital divided into shares and therefore cannot issue bearer shares.

160. In contrast, international companies are permitted to issue bearer shares under the ICA. Despite this, the FSC runs a policy (in place until such time as the legislation is amended to extinguish bearer shares, see paragraph 164) which prohibits the registration of any company with bearer shares.

161. In 2016 and 2017, the FSC monitored international companies with bearer shares that were managed by licensed trustee companies, reviewing the nature and purpose of both the company and the structures with which they were placed, the records relating to beneficial ownership and bearers, and conducted independent checks on those recorded.

162. The FSC released a policy (non-binding) on 15 November 2017 encouraging the Cook Islands' legal persons to phase out bearer instruments by 1 July 2018 for conversion, redemption or surrender of existing bearer instruments. There were four companies with bearer shares in 2018. Although there is still a provision for issuance of bearer shares in the ICA, the Cook Islands reports that the last company with bearer shares converted these in 2019 and no companies have been registered with bearer shares since then. The FSC reviews the share registers of international companies as part of its inspections of trustee companies and also requires any company to notify it if bearer shares have been issued when renewing their annual certificates.
$^{27}$ The number of issues found by the FSC with international and domestic companies ownership records was not separately provided between the two types of company, this is a combined figure.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: COOK ISLANDS 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

163. In the event that any bearer share was to be issued, section 35A of the ICA requires that it must be delivered to and held by a custodian and the custodian cannot hold the share until it has received satisfactory evidence of the identity of the person for whom they will hold the share in custody. $^{28}$ The custodian must be a licensed financial institution in the Cook Islands and will therefore be subject to the CDD requirements in the FTRA, which now also add to the requirements of the Regulations issued in 2004.

164. According to the FSC, trustee companies are under an expectation that in the event that any client company issued bearer shares, this would prompt legislation to be put forward to extinguish such shares. Furthermore, the relevant trustee company would be put on an enhanced monitoring program in the interim. There is therefore no appetite among international companies and their trustee companies to reintroduce bearer shares, which has also limited the priority given to amend the law to permanently remove the possibility. In any event, there is currently no impediment to transparency related to bearer shares in the Cook Islands. Nevertheless, it remains legally possible for international companies to issue bearer shares in the Cook Islands. The Cook Islands should ensure that ownership information is available in the event that bearer shares are issued (see Annex 1).
A.1.3 Partnerships
Types of Partnerships

165. The following types of partnerships may be established under the Cook Islands' laws: (i) domestic partnerships; (ii) international partnerships and (iii) limited partnerships. In addition, this section also covers foreign partnerships. None of the forms of partnership is a legal entity separate from the individual partners that comprise the partnership.

166. Partnership law in the Cook Islands for domestic entities is governed primarily by a New Zealand enactment, the Partnership Act 1908 (PA). That Act defines a partnership as “the relation which subsists between persons carrying on a business in common with a view to profit” (PA, s. 4(1)). A partnership is a distinct commercial entity for accounting purposes, with each partner jointly and severally liable for the liabilities of the partnership. These partnerships are sometimes referred to as general partnerships. In practice, about 100 domestic partnerships are commonly operating small businesses owned by and comprised of partners who are local tax residents. The partnerships are usually operating small grocery, food or short-term accommodation businesses.
167. The International Partnership Act 1984 (IPA 1984) provides for the creation of two types of partnerships (see also 2015 Report, paragraph 111):
i) international partnership – every partner is jointly and severally liable for the liabilities of the partnership (IPA, s. 22)

ii) limited partnership – every general partner is jointly and severally liable for the liabilities of the partnership, but a limited partner is generally only liable to contribute money or money's worth to the common stock, as capital (IPA, s. 62).

168. At registration, every partner in an international or limited partnership must be non-resident in the Cook Islands. As at 31 March 2025, there were three international partnerships and no limited partnerships in the Cook Islands.

$^{28}$ Section 35A applies to bearer instruments, which are defined to mean any bearer share, warrant to bearer or any other membership interest transferable by delivery, and any form of bearer security issued by an international company, including bearer debentures, bearer bonds and share warrants to bearer.

Identity Information Requirements

169. The creation of an international or limited partnership in the Cook Islands requires registration with the Registrar of Partnerships within the FSC. The registration of these partnerships must be arranged through a trustee company. At registration, one of the partners of an international partnership or limited partnership must be a trustee company or an international company of the kind described at paragraphs 59 to 61. After registration and before commencement of business, details of all partners of limited partnerships (but not international partnerships) must be submitted to the Registrar. Both types of partnership must have a registered office, which must be the registered office in the Cook Islands of the partner that is a trustee company or international company (which, if the latter, will also be the registered office of a trustee company). A trustee company is therefore always engaged at creation and on an ongoing basis for international and limited partnerships and is required to conduct CDD on the partnership and keep this up to date as has been described for companies from paragraph 142.

170. In addition, the conduct of onshore business by an international partnership or limited partnership is governed by the Development Investment Act and is subject to registration with the Business Trade and Investment Board. The information to be filed on registration, and annually thereafter, includes detailed ownership information, with the names, addresses and passport numbers of all legal owners of the shares of the partnership income (Development Investment Act, s. 34 and Regulation 3(d) of the Development Investment Regulations 1996). None of the currently registered international partnerships are carrying on business in the Cook Islands.

171. All accounts and records of an international partnership or limited partnership must be retained for a period of not less than six years following the completion of the transaction to which the records and underlying documentation relate (IPA, s. 7). International partnerships and limited partnerships are not subject to Cook Islands taxation and therefore there are no requirements for them to furnish returns on income (IPA, s. 72). Consequently, no international partnership or limited partnership has reason to register with the RMD or apply for an RMD number, and none have done so.

172. There are no direct registration requirements for domestic partnerships. As explained at paragraphs 70 and 71, taxpayers with assessable income generally must file a tax return and administratively a tax return is not processed until an RMD number (tax identification number, ITA s. 218) is issued, which may be seen as fulfilling the function of a registration system. However, there is no comprehensive requirement to apply for an RMD number. In the case of partnerships, a further layer of uncertainty arises in that these legal arrangements are not “taxpayers” as the Cook Islands levies income tax only on the partners and not the partnership. No penalty has been identified in the Income Tax Act that would be available where a partnership fails to apply for an RMD number. Nevertheless, partnerships may apply for an RMD number for various reasons, such as for importing goods, registering for VAT or to meet obligations as an employer.

173. As of January 2026, there were 152 partnerships registered with the RMD, although, following analysis in February 2026, the RMD identified that 71 of these should be deactivated due to conversions to companies or sole traders, cessation or never commencing business. A more up-to-date number is therefore considered to be 81. These would generally be domestic partnerships, although the distinction between domestic and foreign (if any) is not made in the registration. The application form requires each partner to be identified and verified with identity documents specified, such as a passport, a Cook Islands driver's licence or a birth certificate in the case of individuals, or a certificate of incorporation or trust deed in the case of companies and trusts, respectively.

174. Each partner is separately assessable and liable for the tax payable on their share of the partnership income (ITA, s. 11), and every person chargeable with income tax under the Income Tax Act must furnish a return of income (ITA, ss. 2 and 8). Section 11(1)(b)(i) of the Income Tax Act requires that partners also file a joint return of the income of the partnership, setting forth the shares of each partner therein, but in practice the RMD does not enforce this and instead is content with the requirement that each partner file details of their partnership income in their individual tax return. In the case of a business jointly carried on by a husband and wife, section 11(2) would generally formalise this arrangement as they are only considered to be in partnership if there is a bona fide deed of partnership. The individual tax return requires the name of the partnership (which could be a trading name) and the partner's share of the net income from the partnership. The identity of the natural person partners in a domestic partnership is therefore required to be provided to the RMD.

175. Each partner themselves will also have the identity of the other partners under the partnership agreement and can be compelled to provide that information to the RMD on request under section 220 of the Income Tax Act (see Element B.1.1).

176. However, if every partner in a domestic partnership is either a company or an individual acting in the role of trustee in respect of their interest in the partnership, neither the company tax return nor the trust tax return requires information on the partnership. It is therefore possible for a domestic partnership to exist and be in compliance with tax requirements (other than the non-enforced requirement to file a tax return for the partnership) without the RMD being informed of its existence or the identity of any of the partners. All domestic partnerships currently registered with the RMD are comprised entirely of individuals. Therefore, given the nature and use of domestic partnerships in the Cook Islands, there is no current gap and the possibility of a gap arising in the future is very low if there is no change in practices. Nevertheless, the Cook Islands should ensure that all domestic partnerships relevant under the standard are identifiable through tax registrations and/or through the filing of tax returns (see Annex 1).

177. To the extent that partnership information is filed in applications for an RMD number or in the tax returns of partners, there is no explicit obligation on the RMD to retain these records for a specified period. However, the time bar limit on standard tax assessments of four years and ten years for criminal matters would be considered. In practice, the RMD keeps all paper records for at least 20 years and electronic records indefinitely.

178. Foreign partnerships deriving income in the Cook Islands and being at least one third foreign owned must be registered with the Business Trade and Investment Board and file annual returns containing identity information. The individual partners, including the foreign ones, are also required to file annual tax returns, as the partners are taxable individually on their share of the partnership's income (Income Tax Act, s. 8). The foreign partners are taxable on their share of Cook Islands sourced income. No foreign partnerships are currently registered.
Beneficial ownership

179. The standard requires that information in respect of each beneficial owner of a relevant partnership be available. Where any partner is a company or other entity or arrangement, information on the beneficial owners of that entity or arrangement should be available.

180. There is no obligation on the partnership or a partner to maintain such information. There is also no obligation under the tax law or the partnership law to report information on the beneficial ownership of partnerships, except when the Business Trade and Investment Board is involved. Foreign partnerships carrying on business in the Cook Islands must be registered with the Business Trade and Investment Board and information on the identity of partners is obtained through the approval process to qualify as a foreign enterprise and is updated annually as described in paragraph 69. The application form requires identification of the owners of the business, the number of shares held, and the beneficial owner of the shares (which for partnerships is required to be expressed in terms of their share in the capital and profits of the partnership). The instructions require that in the case of a company or trust being a “beneficial owner”, the identity and identification documents are to be provided for the “ultimate beneficiary”. While the application form does not refer to partnerships and partners, a due diligence schedule to the application form indicates that each partner in a partnership should complete the schedule. 181. The Cook Islands' AML framework therefore provides the primary basis for the availability of beneficial ownership on partnerships.

182. As described at paragraph 169, no international or limited partnership can be registered unless the Registrar has received a certificate completed by a trustee company, and an ongoing relationship with a trustee company is required. The beneficial ownership information on international partnerships and limited liability partnerships is therefore kept with licensed trustee companies (who are reporting institutions for the purposes of the FTRA).

183. CDD requirements under section 25 of the FTRA 2017 require reporting institutions to identify and verify any ultimate principal of the customer. As none of the types of partnership that can be formed in the Cook Islands have legal personality, the definition of ultimate principals in the case a legal arrangement is applicable for partnerships.
184. Prior to 4 December 2024, the term “ultimate principal” relevant to legal arrangements was defined as (FTRA 2017, s. 8)
one or more natural persons who ultimately own or effectively control the customer, or on whose behalf a transaction or activity is being conducted and includes:

(iii) in the case of a legal arrangement or similar type of arrangement, the trustee, or any natural person who exercises effective control over the legal arrangement including through a chain of control or ownership.
185. The definition was not inconsistent with the standard, although there was no further guidance on how the definition should apply to the different types of partnerships in practice.

186. The FTRA was amended with effect from 4 December 2024 (see paragraph 127 for the new definition). This was supplemented in the FTRA regulations, and the specification relevant to Cook Islands partnerships can be found in subclauses (6) and (7) of Regulation 6: $^{29}$
(6) ...all of the following natural persons, or natural persons occupying equivalent or similar positions, are deemed to be ultimate principals:
(a) each constituent or settlor
(d) each beneficiary
(e) any other natural persons exercising, directly or indirectly, de facto or de jure, ultimate effective control over the legal arrangement.

(7) If any of the functions of a legal arrangement referred to in subclause (6) are performed by a legal person or legal arrangement, the natural person or persons identified as the ultimate principals of that legal person or legal arrangement are deemed to be the ultimate principals of the legal arrangement.
187. The current requirements in the FTRA for identification of the beneficial owners of partnerships in the Cook Islands are in line with the standard and add clarity.

188. The AML framework ensures the availability of the identity of the partners in, and the beneficial owners of, any international or limited partnership. For domestic and foreign partnerships, this information could be available if there is a relationship with an AML obliged service provider (such as a bank), however there is no legal requirement for engaging on a continuous basis with such a service provider. Even if an AML obliged service provider in the Cook Islands is engaged, this is likely only to be a bank and there is no specified frequency for which the CDD would need to be updated by these entities to ensure that the information held is current (see paragraph 145). Thus, it is not ensured that beneficial ownership information will always be available under the AML law. The Cook Islands is recommended to ensure that adequate, accurate and up-to-date beneficial ownership information in line with the standard is always available for all relevant partnerships.

Oversight and Enforcement

189. Compliance with obligations on availability of both identity and beneficial ownership information of partnerships is monitored mainly through AML supervision. The availability of identity information on domestic partnerships is also supervised by the RMD.

190. Registration of international partnerships and limited partnerships must be arranged through a trustee company who, in turn, is subject to FTRA obligations (IPA 1984, ss. 10 and 55). These partnerships must also have an ongoing relationship with a trustee company. Failure to comply with any legal obligations imposed by the IPA is an offence and, on conviction, punishable with a fine not exceeding NZD 10 000 (EUR 5 040) and/or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year (IPA 1984, s. 79). The FSC is responsible for compliance with the IPA, and in conjunction with the FIU is also responsible for supervising partnership service providers (the trustee companies) to ensure compliance with all regulatory requirements, including the obligation to obtain and maintain identity information and the retention of these records as required under the FTRA Act 2017. The supervisory activities conducted by the FSC in relation to the compliance of trustee companies with the FTRA and other laws are described at paragraphs 106 and 155.

191. While no international partnerships were specifically selected in the review period for these activities, this was because reviews are based on selection of clients of the trustee companies and it happened that none of the selected clients were connected to the three international partnerships in existence. The reviews nevertheless do adequately test the compliance of each trustee company with their CDD obligations in general under the FTRA.

192. More broadly, as concerns CDD practices of banks with customers that are international or domestic partnerships, specific statistics have not been provided but partnerships and their partners are covered in general by the supervision activities with banks described in paragraphs 156 and 323.

193. The RMD is responsible for the monitoring of availability of identity information on domestic partnerships. Under tax law, a person who fails to file a tax return or gives false information is liable to a fine not exceeding NZD 10 000 (EUR 5 040) and not less than NZD 5 000 (EUR 2 520) (ITA, s. 206).

194. The RMD states that of the 152 partnerships registered for tax purposes (81 considered to be active, see paragraph 172173), only 57 partnerships had one or more of the partners file a tax return or were newly created and therefore were not yet due to file tax returns. The RMD monitors the filing obligations by cross-referencing the filing of income tax returns of partners with the registration of partnerships for VAT and PAYE purposes (pay-as-you-earn withholding tax on salary payment to employees of the partnership). However, it is clear that some of the domestic partnerships registered with the RMD do not have partners filing tax returns that identify or update information on the partnership. The RMD conducted audits on 14 domestic partnerships during the review period, although these focussed on VAT and would have only incidentally considered identity information, if at all. Furthermore, no compliance activities have been identified that would support the RMD's understanding on whether all domestic partnerships have registered in practice. As noted above, the materiality of the gap is low for EOIR purposes.

A.1.4 Trusts

196. The Cook Islands allows for the creation of common law trusts (domestic trusts) and of international trusts under the International Trusts Act and recognises foreign trusts. The Cook Islands has adopted the equity laws of the United Kingdom and New Zealand, which allow for the creation of trust relationships. There were 111 domestic trusts and no foreign trusts registered with the RMD on 12 February 2026. There were 7 licensed trustee companies administering 2 218 international trusts in July 2025. The population of trusts is stable, as there were 84 domestic trusts and 2 201 international trusts in April 2022, with the same number of licensees.
Identity Information

197. The Cook Islands requires the availability of identity information on the participants in international trusts through the CDD obligations imposed on trustee companies under the international trusts and AML laws, and through tax law in the case of domestic trusts.

198. There are no explicit requirements in statutory law for domestic trusts to obtain and retain information on the identity of parties to the trust, but information may nevertheless be available with the RMD or with the trustee.

199. A common law trust settled in the Cook Islands is generally liable for income tax on assessable income. The Income Tax Act has specific rules for foreign trusts, which are defined to be any trust that at a moment in time has no settlor that has been resident in the Cook Islands since the time that a settlement to the trust was first made. A tax return is required for a domestic or foreign trust if it has income assessable in the Cook Islands in a tax year.

200. The impetus and process for trusts to register with the RMD is the same as described for companies in paragraphs 70 to 71 and for partnerships in paragraph 172 – an application for an RMD number may be filed by the trustee but is not comprehensively required of all relevant trusts. If filed, the application requires the trust deed and identity documentation for the trustee to be provided (but not for any other person such as a settlor, protector or beneficiary).

201. A trustee of a trust with income assessable by the Cook Islands must file an annual tax return for the trust and the prescribed tax return must disclose settlor and beneficiary information. The trust tax return requires identification of the settlor(s), trustee(s) and beneficiaries including their name, RMD number and address, though it is unclear whether this means that every party to the trust must have an RMD number through completing the application and identification process or whether the trustee could compel other parties to the trust to obtain an RMD number if they do not already have such a number. These requirements are imposed by the prescribed form and are not directly specified in the ITA. The form does not require information on any protectors of the trust or further information on the parties to the trust in the event that they are legal entities or legal arrangements.

202. Under common law applicable in the Cook Islands, a trustee has a duty to know the terms of the trust. This includes having documentation relating to or affecting the trust property as it comes under their control. Identity information of settlor and beneficiaries (or the identification of a class of beneficiaries) would normally be known to trustees in order for them to perform their duties. If relevant, any other person with the ability to exert some control may also be expected to be known to the trustee.

203. Trustees are under a general requirement to maintain account information under section 217 of the Income Tax Act, but this would not necessarily extend to records on the structure and parties to the trust. In the event that a trustee has such information in the Cook Islands, the Collector has the power to access that information under section 219 of the ITA 1997. Section 220 also allows the Collector to compel any person such as a trustee to provide information relevant to the Income tax Act, including for the purpose of giving effect to an international agreement. The effectiveness of this power would depend on whether, as a question of fact, the trustee possesses or controls the information sought.

204. Cook Islands law recognises foreign trusts generally. Under section 17 of the Development Investment Act, any foreign enterprise (including domestic and foreign trusts) with more than one third foreign ownership and wishing to invest in or carry on a business in the Cook Islands must register with the BTIB. The information to be filed on registration, and annually thereafter, includes detailed ownership information, such as the names, addresses and passport numbers of all participants to the trust (Development Investment Act, s. 34 and Regulations 3(d) and 8 of the Development Investment Regulations). However, foreign trusts with less than one third foreign ownership or foreign trusts investing exclusively abroad would not be subject to such registration requirements. In the case of a foreign trust, a Cook Islands resident may act as a trustee, however, should the foreign trust have a resident trustee and at any point in time a settlor is resident, then the trust must submit a return on world-wide income (ITA 1997, s. 77, as amended by the Income Tax Amendment Act 2017), i.e. the obligation does not apply if no settlor is resident in the Cook Islands.

205. In order to qualify as an international trust, a trust (whether settled in the Cook Islands or elsewhere) must be registered on the International Trust Register with the FSC and, on so doing, becomes subject to the provisions of the International Trusts Act 1984 (ITA, s. 15). A trust does not qualify for registration if any beneficiary is domiciled or ordinarily resident in the Cook Islands (ITA, ss. 2 and 22) and in the event that the Registrar reasonably believes that any beneficiary of a registered international trust has subsequently become domiciled or ordinarily resident in the Cook Islands, it may deregister the trust. Only a licensed trustee company may register an international trust. A trustee company is a reporting entity under the Financial Transaction Reporting Act 2017 and therefore subject to the requirements of the Act to maintain identity information on all its trust customers.

206. Licensed trustee companies (and financial institutions) are required to keep CDD information (as outlined above) up to date and monitor any subsequent information to ensure it stays in line with what they understand of the structure and those involved (FTRA 2017, s. 32). Prior to 4 December 2024, the scope of the persons to be identified according to the AML/CFT legislation included the trustee or any natural person exercising ultimate effective control on a trust, including through a chain of control or ownership, but did not explicitly require identification of the settlor and protector. Amendments to the FTRA and its regulations with effect from 4 December 2024 now explicitly specify these among the roles that must be identified in relation to the trust. The requirements to identify participants to the trust are now in line with standard. The CDD procedures must ensure that the reporting institution verifies the identification information using reliable independent source documents (FTRA 2017, s. 25(2)). If a trust service arrangement is terminated with a licensed service provider, the service provider is required to retain records on that trust arrangement for six years.
Availability of beneficial ownership information

207. Requirements related to beneficial ownership information of trusts are mainly found in the FTRA, as the requirements under the tax law do not ensure the availability of complete beneficial ownership information.

208. International trusts must meet the requirements under the relevant international acts, including the requirement that they must have a Cook Islands licensed trustee company as trustee or registered agent. The trustee company (which is a reporting institution for the purposes of the FTRA) must fulfil its AML requirements prior to registering the international trust. The trustee company is required to retain all related records for six years after its relationship with the trust ends.

209. Where a customer is not a natural person, the reporting institution must identify and verify any ultimate principal of the customer and verify the legal status of the customer, using relevant information obtained from reliable independent sources, and obtain sufficient information to understand the nature of the customer's business and control structure. As noted in paragraph 184, “ultimate principal” includes any natural person who exercises effective control over the legal arrangement, including through a chain of control or ownership.
210. The term “ultimate principal” is defined in section 8 of the FTRA. Prior to 4 December 2024, that section defined ultimate principals of a trust to be:
one or more natural persons who ultimately own or effectively control the customer, or on whose behalf a transaction or activity is being conducted and includes:

(iii) in the case of a legal arrangement or similar type of arrangement, the trustee, or any natural person who exercises effective control over the legal arrangement including through a chain of control or ownership.

211. Inconsistent with the standard, the AML definition applicable in the Cook Islands prior to 4 December 2024 only required identification of the trustee or any natural persons exercising ultimate effective control of the trust but did not explicitly require identification of the settlor and protector, and therefore also did not capture any natural persons behind these roles in a trust if held by persons that are not themselves natural persons.

212. The definition of ultimate principal in the FTRA was amended with effect from 4 December 2024 (reproduced at paragraph 127 in this report). The regulations were also amended at the same time to expand upon the meaning and insofar as is relevant for trusts it means:
(6) ...all of the following natural persons, or natural persons occupying equivalent or similar positions, are deemed to be ultimate principals:
(a) each constituent or settlor
(b) each trustee
(c) each protector (if any)
(d) each beneficiary
(e) any other natural persons exercising, directly or indirectly, de facto or de jure, ultimate effective control over the legal arrangement.

(7) If any of the functions of a legal arrangement referred to in subclause (6) are performed by a legal person or legal arrangement, the natural person or persons identified as the ultimate principals of that legal person or legal arrangement are deemed to be the ultimate principals of the legal arrangement.
213. The current definition applicable to trusts is in line with the standard.

214. There is no legal requirement for a domestic trustee of a domestic or foreign trust to have a local bank account, nor is there any other requirement to engage an AML-obliged person. Therefore, in situations where an AML-obliged person has not been engaged, beneficial ownership information would not be available and in situations where an AML-obliged person has been engaged, particularly when the only such engagement is with a bank, beneficial ownership information may not be accurate and up to date due to the lack of specified frequency for updating CDD (see paragraph 145).

215. For domestic trusts, the requirement to keep and report trust information arises only if and when the trustees file annual returns of income and financial reports. Before that, there are no statutory requirements for domestic trusts to obtain and retain information on beneficial ownership. As described in paragraph 201, the trust tax return requires identification of the settlor(s), trustee(s) and beneficiaries including their name, RMD number and address. The Collector has the power to access identity information held by a trustee; however, it is not assured that further information on beneficial owners will be held or available to the trustee in the event that parties to the trust are legal entities or legal arrangements. Tax law therefore does not ensure that complete beneficial ownership information will be available and in line with the standard.

216. The identification of participants to domestic trusts and foreign trusts with a resident trustee is not ensured when they do not meet some criteria in the Income Tax Act and do not have a relationship with an AML-obliged person.

217. Even if an AML-obliged person in the Cook Islands is engaged (which is not required in all cases), there is no specified frequency for which the CDD would need to be updated to ensure that the information held is current.

218. Thus, it is not ensured that adequate, accurate and up-to-date beneficial ownership information will always be available under tax or AML law. Oversight and Enforcement

219. The RMD has not had to obtain identity or beneficial ownership information on domestic trusts in practice, however it is likely that the AML framework would be one source of information in the event that it became necessary. In relation to CDD practices of banks with customers that are domestic trusts, the supervision activities with banks described in paragraphs 156 and 320 are indirectly relevant in demonstrating the adequacy of supervision by the FSC, including for trusts generally, although only one domestic trust came up as a bank customer in the file sampling owing to the proportionally small number of these in existence. In any case, the AML framework cannot be a comprehensive source of information on domestic trusts as they are not required to have a relationship with an AML-obliged person.

220. Tax law provides the main source of information on trust participants and potentially for some beneficial ownership information, the latter being subject to the limitations described in paragraph 215. The RMD is responsible for compliance by domestic and foreign trusts with tax law, and the same penalties apply as mentioned in paragraph 193 for non-filing and providing incorrect information. The RMD states that of the 75 trusts registered for tax purposes and that were not deceased estates, only 15 had a tax return filed for the 2024 year. It is clear that many of the trusts registered with the RMD are not filing tax returns that identify or update information on the trust. Furthermore, no compliance activities have been identified that would support the RMD's understanding on whether all relevant trusts have registered in practice or that those trusts that are registered continue to exist in practice (see also paragraph 101 on the RMD's reticence to pursue non-compliance through court action). No audits of any kind were carried out in connection with trusts in the review period.

221. Both the FIU and FSC play a role in the licensing and ongoing monitoring/supervision of trustee companies and their client entities and arrangements to ensure compliance with all regulatory requirements, including the obligation to obtain and maintain legal ownership and identity information and the retention of these records as required under the FTRA 2017, the Trustee Companies Act 2014, International Companies Act 1981-82, International Trusts Act 1984, International Partnerships Act 1984, Limited Liability Companies Act 2008, and Foundations Act 2012.

222. International trusts must register with the Registrar of Trusts and a copy of the trust deed must be provided to the Registrar as part of the registration requirements (ITA, s. 17). A NZD 74 (EUR 38) penalty per month applies for a late filing of the annual renewal of an international trust's registration, calculated according to each month or part thereof that the filing is outstanding (International Trusts (Prescribed Fees) (Amendment) Regulations 2014). The registration and its annual renewal must be arranged through a trustee company who is subject to FTRA obligations and at least one trustee must be in the Cook Islands (ITA, ss. 2 and 15(1)(a)).

A.1.5 Foundations and incorporated societies
Foundations

227. Cook Islands introduced foundations in 2012 pursuant to the Foundations Act 2012. A foundation receives its initial capital from one or more founders, and, at any time after the creation of the foundation, any other person (known as a dedicator) may transfer assets to the foundation (Foundations Act, s. 14). Founders can be nationals or foreigners. The objects of a foundation may be charitable, non-charitable or both. A foundation's object may be to benefit a person or class of persons, to carry out a specified purpose, or both (Foundations Act, s. 7). A foundation may only directly engage in commercial trading if it is incidental to the attainment of the foundation's objects (Foundations Act, s. 35(3)). A foundation will have a council to administer the foundation's assets and carry out its objects (Foundations Act, s. 22).

228. Foundations are not subject to tax in the Cook Islands and are therefore not required to submit a tax return. However, a foundation must have a trustee company residing in the Cook Islands as its registered agent, and which will provide the foundation's registered office in the Cook Islands (Foundations Act, s. 27). According to the FSC, there are 46 registered foundations in the Cook Islands as of 31 March 2025.

229. The legal framework governing foundations ensures the availability of identity information through the Foundations Act and through the obligations imposed on trustee companies by the FTRA. Information is also updated where a change to the governance of the foundation occurs, and as beneficiaries become entitled to distributions. Foundations are required to keep documents and records at their registered office, including a register showing the names and addresses of the members of its council and all dedicators to the foundation (Foundations Act, s. 42).

230. An application for the creation and registration of a foundation is submitted by a trustee company resident in the Cook Islands (Foundations Act, s. 4) to the Registrar of Foundations, located in the FSC. The application must be accompanied by the foundation instrument, which sets out the name and objects of the foundation, the beneficiaries to benefit from the foundation (if any), and the name and address of the registered agent (Foundations Act, ss. 7 and 8). The trustee company must also submit a declaration that it is in possession of the foundation rules, which includes the rules governing the appointment and functioning of the council, registered agent, enforcer, dedicators and may set out further details as to the method of determining beneficiaries (Foundations Act, ss. 9 to 13). The records are kept at the Registrar of Foundations for at least ten years upon the dissolution of a foundation (Foundations Act, s. 49).

231. There are no requirements on beneficial ownership information under the Foundations Act 2012. However, a foundation must always have a relationship with a trustee company that is an AML-obliged person and therefore AML law is relevant to the availability of beneficial ownership information on foundations.

232. The CDD requirements under section 25 of the FTRA 2017 require a trustee company to identify and verify any ultimate principal of the foundation. The term “ultimate principal” applicable to foundations (as legal entities) prior to 4 December 2024 is described at paragraph 146. It was doubtful whether the AML law requirements of the Cook Islands ensured that information on beneficial owners of foundations would be available in accordance with the standard. While members of the foundation council (and by extension any persons with the authority to represent the foundation) were captured by the requirement to identify any person who controlled the foundation acting directly or indirectly, and acting individually or jointly, the beneficiaries (where applicable) did not appear to be covered.

233. The definition of ultimate principal in the FTRA and its Regulations was amended with effect from 4 December 2024, as described at paragraph 149. In addition, provisions were added to Regulation 6 to clarify the meaning specifically for foundations:
(8) In the case of a foundation, all of the following natural persons are deemed to be ultimate principals:
(a) each founder
(b) each member of the board of the foundation board
(c) each beneficiary
(d) any other natural person who, directly or indirectly, de facto or de jure, exercises ultimate effective control over the foundation.

(9) If any of the functions of a foundation referred to in subclause (8) are performed by a legal person or legal arrangement, the natural person or persons identified as the ultimate principals of that legal person or legal arrangement are deemed to be the ultimate principals of the foundation.
234. The current definition applicable to foundations is in line with the standard.

235. Oversight and enforcement activities by the FSC for legal and beneficial ownership information on foundations are integrated with those described for the AML framework relevant to companies under A.1.1. Trustee company client files on foundations are reviewed for compliance with the FTRA. During the review period, there were 25 foundations reviewed in those activities. No issues with foundations were identified.
