Incorporated societies

236. An incorporated society can be created under the Incorporated Societies Act, i.e. any society consisting of not less than 15 persons associated for any lawful but not pecuniary gain (ISA, s. 3). The application for registration is to be made to the Registrar in accordance with the ISA. There were 264 incorporated societies registered with the Registrar of Incorporated Societies (Ministry of Justice) in the Cook Islands as at 6 February 2026.

237. The law provides that persons are not deemed to be associated for pecuniary gain merely because the society itself makes a pecuniary gain, so long as the gain is not divided among or received by any member (ISA, s. 4. This allows for pecuniary gains to be made that are incidental or subsidiary to the overall non-profit purpose of the society, so long as the pecuniary gains are not intended to bring the society into profit overall. If a society were to carry out any act of such a nature that the members would be deemed to be associated for pecuniary gain, the society would be subject to a penalty of NZD 500 (EUR 252), each member who assists or takes part may be penalised NZD 100 (EUR 50) and each such member will be jointly and severally liable for all debts and obligations incurred by the society in consequence of the act. Persons are also not deemed to be associated for pecuniary gain merely because the property of the society may be divided among the members on its dissolution. However, the possibility of any gain remaining is constrained by the overarching requirement that the society is set up and operates for a non-profit purpose throughout its existence. There is no prohibition on incorporated societies operating outside the Cook Islands.

238. Incorporated societies are not directly exempt from tax, however the types of income that such societies might derive (if any) is likely to be exempt, namely income of societies established for religious, charitable, sporting or other community purposes.

239. The application for registration must identify the name, residential and postal address of each subscriber that is an individual. Body corporates are permitted to subscribe and must be identified by name, corporate registration number (if any) and the address of its registered office and postal address must be provided. Membership information does not include beneficial ownership information, and it is not required to be updated with the Registrar. The society must maintain, at its registered office, a register of members that includes their name, address, occupation and the date that they became a member. The registered office must be in the Cook Islands. There is no requirement that members be resident in the Cook Islands. The register is only required to be provided to the Registrar if requested to do so. Annual financial statements are required to be filed with the Registrar, but this does not include member information.

240. Taking into account their nature and purposes, incorporated societies in the Cook Islands are not materially relevant for EOIR purposes given that they are formed at a local level for community purposes.
Availability of identity and beneficial ownership information on foundations and incorporated societies in EOIR practice
241. No EOI requests were received during the review period in respect of foundations or incorporated societies.

A.2 Accounting records
Jurisdictions should ensure that reliable accounting records are kept for all relevant entities and arrangements.

242. The 2015 Report concluded that the legal framework for maintaining reliable accounting records with underlying documentation by all relevant legal persons and arrangements was in place in the Cook Islands but certain aspects of the legal implementation of the element needed improvement. The element was rated Largely Compliant.

243. The Cook Islands was recommended under both the 2015 Report and the 2022 Phase 1 Report to require limited liability companies, international trusts and foundations to keep underlying documentation in respect of all transactions. In addition, both reports concluded that the Cook Islands should ensure that the failure of a foundation to maintain all accounting records and underlying documentation for at least five years be subject to effective penalties. The recommendations remain unaddressed.

244. Further deficiencies have been identified. The accounting records retention requirements are not clear in the case of domestic companies that cease to exist. Under the company law, a liquidator may be engaged and, if so, is only required to maintain the records for a period of at least one year. If a domestic company ceases to exist without the engagement of a liquidator, no person is made responsible for retaining the records under company law or tax law.

245. Supervision of the international sector is relatively robust and sufficiently ensures the availability of reliable accounting records with underlying documentation for companies and arrangements in that sector. Availability in the domestic sector relies on the tax framework and while there is some supervision, it requires improvements. In practice, the requests that the Cook Islands receive are consistently in connection with the international sector. There were no requests made or identified as being in connection with the domestic sector during the review period. However, while requests made or identified as being in connection with the domestic sector have not been received in recent years, if ever, some doubt arises on whether the information would be available in practice if requested.

246. During the review period, the Cook Islands received seven requests with accounting information in the scope of the requests, all related to entities and arrangements in the international sector. No issues were reported by the Cook Islands or its peers in obtaining such information in practice.
247. The conclusions are as follows:
Legal and regulatory framework: In place, but certain aspects of the legal implementation of the element need improvement

text: A.2.1 General requirements and A.2.2 Underlying documentation

248. In the Cook Islands, the requirement to keep accounting records in accordance with the standard is ensured by a combination of the company, tax and AML law requirements. The various legal regimes are analysed below.
Company Law
249. The directors of domestic companies must ensure that accounting records are kept in compliance with the Companies Act requirements. In particular, the accounting records must:
\- correctly record the company’s transactions
\- at any time, enable the company's financial position to be determined with reasonable accuracy

\- enable directors to ensure that within four months after the company's balance date, the financial statements give a true and fair view of the matters, comply with any applicable regulations made under this Act and be dated and signed on behalf of the company by the director(s)
\- enable the company's financial statements to be readily and properly audited (regardless of whether the company is actually required to prepare financial statements) (CA 2017, s. 159).

250. The accounting records must contain entries of money received and spent each day and the matters to which the money relates, a record of company's assets and liabilities, a record of all transactions affecting the assets and liabilities, all sales and purchases of goods and services (CA 2017, s. 159(2)). In addition, domestic companies are required to keep all underlying documents of transactions under tax law as long as they carry on business or receive income other than salary or wages (see paragraph 267). Accounting records are not required to be filed with the Registrar.

251. The accounting records must be kept at the registered office of the company or another place in the Cook Islands that is not its registered office, provided the company has given the Registrar a notice of the location of the records within 10 days after the records are first kept there (CA 2017, s. 145(1)(2)). The accounting records must be kept for the current accounting period and for the last seven completed accounting periods of the company. The Registrar may approve by notice in writing to the company a shorter period than seven completed accounting periods (CA 2017, s. 144). There were no such exceptions granted as per March 2026. The Cook Islands authorities state that approval would only be given in exceptional circumstances, such as if a company has ceased operations or is being wound up, and that approval would not be granted in a way that could compromise regulatory oversight or the availability of accounting information. Nevertheless, the Cook Islands should ensure that any approvals to retain accounting records for less than seven completed accounting periods does not interfere with the availability of accounting information as required by the standard (see Annex 1).
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: COOK ISLANDS 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

252. A domestic company that has 10 or more shareholders must prepare financial statements (CA 2017, s. 161). A company with less than 10 shareholders may be required by a shareholder to prepare financial statements under certain conditions. If financial statements are required to be prepared, they must be audited by a qualified and independent auditor.
253. International companies are required to keep accounts and records relating to:
• all sums of money received and expended by the company
• all sales and purchases of goods by the company
• all assignments of rights or assumption of liabilities by the company
• all transactions of the company affecting the assets or liabilities of the company and
• the assets and liabilities of the company (ICA, s. 113(1)).

254. The keeping of accounts and records must be “sufficient to show and explain the international company’s transactions, which gives a true and accurate record” of the above details, and that “will at any time enable the financial position of an international company to be determined with reasonable accuracy” (ICA, s. 113). The resident secretary of an international company must keep the company records in the Cook Islands for a period of not less than six years following the completion of the transaction to which the records and underlying documentation relate. Thus, the ICA explicitly refers to the requirement to maintain both accounting records and underlying documentation. Financial statements are not required to be audited if members resolve that an auditor not be appointed.
255. A limited liability company must keep accounting records that are sufficient to show and explain its transactions, which give a true and accurate record of:
• all sums of money received and expended by the company
• all sales and purchases of goods by the company
• all assignments of rights or assumption of liabilities by the company
• all transactions of the company affecting the assets or liabilities of the company and
• the assets and liabilities of the company (LLCA, s. 31A(1)).
256. All the records must at any time enable the financial position of a limited liability company to be determined with reasonable accuracy.

257. The accounts of a limited liability company must be retained by the resident agent within the Cook Islands either in hard copy or in electronic format with hard copy easily and immediately printable (LLCA, s. 31A(2)). More specifically, the accounts must be kept at the registered office of the limited liability company (which is the business address of the registered agent). Such records are subject to inspection and copying at the reasonable request, and at the expense, of any member. The records must be maintained for six years following dissolution of the company. This is the only time limit specified, and the Cook Islands confirms that records must continue to be retained without time limit so long as the limited liability company continues in existence.

258. Although limited liability companies are required to keep accurate records of expenditures, sales and purchases and all transactions affecting assets and liabilities, as concluded in both the 2015 Report and the 2022 Phase 1 Report, there is no explicit reference to the requirement to maintain all underlying source documentation evidencing these transactions, such as invoices and contracts. This remains the case. However, the FSC, from its reviews of trustee companies and clients that are limited liability companies, observes that in practice disbursements from a limited liability companies will normally have a resolution of the managers, related invoice, remittance details confirmation and instructions for payment for any transactions.

259. Foreign companies are required to keep reliable accounting records, including underlying documents, for at least five years (see section on tax law). In practice, accounting records are required to be submitted to the Business Trade and Investment Board (BTIB) when it is considering a new application, in particular to assess the sufficiency of assets and level of borrowing. Financial statements are also required to be filed with the BTIB each year thereafter.
Partnerships, trusts and foundations

260. The International Partnership Amendment Act 2013 (IPA) foresees an obligation to maintain accounting records. International partnerships and limited partnerships must keep accounting records that are sufficient to show and explain the partnership's transactions, which gives a true and accurate record of:
• all sums of money received and expended by the partnership
• all sales and purchases of goods by the partnership
• all assignments of rights or assumption of liabilities by the partnership
• all transactions of the company affecting the assets or liabilities of the partnership and
\- the assets and liabilities of the partnership and that will at any time enable the financial position of the partnership to be determined with reasonable accuracy (section 7A).

261. The IPA requires that the accounts and records be retained within the Cook Islands by the trustee company which is the partner or provides the registered office for a partner. Section 7A(4) requires that the accounts and records must be retained within the Cook Islands, for a period of not less than six years following the completion of the transaction to which the records and underlying documentation relate. Thus, the IPA explicitly refers to the requirement to maintain both accounting records and underlying documentation. Any partner of an international partnership, or any general partner of a limited partnership, that fails to take all reasonable steps to secure compliance with this obligation, commits an offence against the IPA (IPA 1984, ss. 7A(3), see para. 288).

262. Foreign partnerships need to be registered with the Business Trade and Investment Board (BTIB), albeit only if foreign partner(s) have more than a one third interest in the capital or profits of the partnership. No partnerships of this kind are currently registered. The individual partners, including the foreign ones, are also required to file annual tax returns, as the partners are taxed individually on their share of the partnership's income (see paragraph 178). No foreign partnerships are currently registered with the RMD. As is the case for foreign companies (see paragraph 259) accounting records must be provided by foreign partnerships when filing applications to the BTIB and annual financial statements filed thereafter.

263. The Trustee Act does not explicitly require the keeping of accounting records. Under the common law, however, there is a general duty on trustees to maintain proper accounts and records, which is linked to the duty to inform beneficiaries.

264. The International Trusts Amendment Act 2013 introduced an obligation on trustees of an international trust to maintain accounting records. The trustee must ensure that there is, at the registered office of the international trust, a true, accurate and current record of:
• income of the trust, whether in cash or kind
• assets held by the trust
• assets made available for use by any beneficiary of the trust
• advances made by the trust
• distributions made

\- all transactions of the trust affecting its assets or liabilities and which will at any time enable the financial position of the international trust to be determined with reasonable accuracy (section 27C).

265. Foundations are required to keep financial records at their registered office under the Foundations Act 2012 (s. 42(2)). Foundations must keep financial records which (i) enable the financial position of the foundation to be determined with reasonable accuracy at any time, and (ii) allow financial statements to be prepared (s. 43(1)). The records must be kept for a minimum period of six years (s. 43(4)).

266. The requirements in paragraphs 264 and 265 are broad enough to require records of all sums of money received and expended and the matters in respect of which the receipt and expenditure takes place, all sales and purchases and other transactions, and the assets and liabilities of international trusts and foundations. However, as was found in both the 2015 Report and the 2022 Phase 1 Report, there is no general requirement to maintain underlying documentation evidencing the transactions of international trusts and foundations, such as invoices and contracts. This remains the case.
Tax law

267. The Income Tax Act imposes record keeping requirements which apply to “every person carrying on business or receiving income other than salary or wages” (ITA, s. 217(1)). This includes domestic and foreign companies. It also applies to domestic partnerships. These general tax obligations equally apply to resident trustees with respect to income and allowable deductions pertaining to domestic trusts, as well as to beneficiaries of any domestic trust deriving income sourced in the Cook Islands, who are required to furnish annual tax returns (ITA, ss. 2 and 8).

268. The records must be sufficient “to enable that person’s assessable income and allowable deductions to be readily ascertained by the Collector” (ITA, s. 217(1)). In particular, such records include underlying documents such as the asset schedule and “books of account, recording receipts documents of income or expenditure or purchases or sales, and also includes vouchers, invoices, receipts, and such other documents as are necessary to verify the entries in any such books of account and, in the case of an agent, records of all transactions carried out on behalf of that agent’s principal” (ITA, ss. 60(2) and 217(3)). The ledgers and journals must adequately explain each transaction.

269. There is no requirement in the Income Tax Act to maintain these records in the Cook Islands, however it is required under company law (see paragraph 251) albeit that this obligation is to be supervised by a different authority. The tax law is the main source of accounting obligations for domestic and foreign partnerships and trusts. Tax law also requires all partners in relevant partnerships, to annually submit some accounting information to the RMD, see paragraph 271, which provides some immediate availability to the RMD. Finally, a person who fails to keep records commits an offence (ITA, s. 217(4)) and would effectively need to provide such records in the Cook Islands (irrespective of where they were kept and whether they complied with company law) in order to prove their compliance with the tax law.

270. Resident trustees of foreign trusts and beneficiaries of foreign trusts, and partners of foreign partnership deriving income from the Cook Islands are required to furnish annual tax returns (ITA, ss. 2, 8, 11, 80 and 83). Such trustees, partners and beneficiaries are, therefore, required to keep reliable accounting records, including underlying documents, for at least five years.

271. The annual tax return for companies explicitly requires the attachment of a “profit and loss account,” which is understood to mean financial statements (i.e. including a balance sheet). The trust tax return requires “financial statements” to be furnished with the tax return. The RMD actively encourages this filing requirement and is generally able to enforce it when tax returns are filed in paper form or by email. In contrast, returns filed through the online portal may be accepted and processed without financial statements being included. The decision to process a tax return without financial statements is risk based. The RMD estimates that around 80% of company returns include financial statements. There is no partnership tax return, but each partner required to file a tax return in the Cook Islands is expected to include financial statements of the partnership with their tax return. However, this does not always occur, as the RMD has identified that only 38 of the 57 partnerships with a partner filing a tax return had financial statements attached. Information has not been provided in relation to filing of financial statements with trust returns.

Conclusion

272. In summary, the gap identified in the 2015 Report in relation to requirements by limited liability companies, international trusts and foundations on keeping all underlying documentation remain. The Cook Islands should require all relevant legal entities and arrangements to keep all underlying documentation in line with the standard.
Companies and arrangements that cease to exist

273. For companies, partnerships and trusts in the international sector that cease to exist, the obligation to retain accounting records and underlying documentation in line with the standard is imposed on the trustee company in the Cook Islands that had the relationship with the company or arrangement at the time it ceased. Retention requirements in relation to domestic and foreign partnerships and trusts are covered by tax law. However, for domestic companies and foundations, it is not clear who would be legally responsible to keep accounting records and underlying documentation when these entities cease to exist or be registered in the Cook Islands. Details follow below.
International sector

274. Where an international company is struck off, the resident secretary must ensure that the books and papers of the company are retained by a trustee company for a period of six years from the striking off (ICA, s. 197(6)). Re-domiciliation of international companies without winding up is possible, in which case the re-domiciled company is removed from the register, however the resident secretary's obligations, including for record keeping, continue as if the company remained registered (ICA, s. 209(5)).

275. When a limited liability company is dissolved, the resident agent must retain specified records of the limited liability company for six years following the dissolution (LLCA, s. 32(2)). The specified records include accounting records. Re-domiciliation of limited liability companies without dissolution is possible, however the resident agent's obligations, including for record keeping, continue as if the company remained registered (ICA, s. 209(5)).

276. When an international trust is terminated, or the Cook Islands trustee is removed or has resigned, each trustee must ensure that the records in the possession of that trustee are retained by that trustee for a period of six years from the date of termination, removal or resignation as the case may be (International Trusts Amendment Act 2013, s. 4(1B)).

277. In the case of international and limited partnerships, the combined effect of subsection 7A(2), which requires the trustee company that is a partner or provides a registered office for a partner to retain the records, and subsection 7A(4), which requires the records and underlying documentation to be retained in the Cook Islands for six years after the transactions to which they relate (see also paragraph 261), effectively requires the trustee company to retain the records for the required period that continues to run after winding up of the partnership. The IPA does not provide for re-domiciliation of international limited partnerships.

278. For foundations, winding up may involve a liquidator and according to the FSC in practice this is always the case when winding up is voluntary, however it might not be done when the process is involuntary, such as striking off for failing to file an annual return. While the Foundations Act provide for the possibility of liquidation, it does not impose an obligation on a liquidator to retain records following liquidation. In addition, while the Foundations Act requires the accounting records to be kept at the registered office or at another place notified to the registered agent, the obligation to keep records is imposed on the foundation and not the registered agent. There is therefore no obligation imposed on the registered agent to continue to hold those records after a foundation is wound up. Furthermore, it is possible for foundations to transfer their registration out of the Cook Islands without being wound up, with no person remaining responsible for retaining accounting records in the Cook Islands.

Domestic and foreign entities

279. A secured creditor of a domestic company may, subject to the debt agreement, appoint a receiver to take control of the property of a company (CA, s. 297). If a receiver is appointed, the receiver must at all times keep accounting records that correctly record and explain the receipts, expenditure and other transactions relating to the property in receivership. The receiver must retain the accounting records for not less than seven years after the receivership ends (CA 2017, s. 311).

280. A domestic company in the Cook Islands may be removed from the register due to: (i) liquidation; (ii) request of a shareholder or another authorised person if the company has ceased business; or (iii) failure to file its annual return or to meet other specified requirements. If a domestic company is liquidated, a liquidator is appointed who must keep the company accounts and records for not less than one year after completion of the liquidation (CA 2017, s. 253). In any other case where a domestic company ceases to exist (i.e. not involving a receiver or liquidator), the Companies Act does not specify any person responsible for retaining company records after the company ceases to exist. The Companies Act does not provide for re-domiciliation of domestic companies.

281. Section 217(2) of the Income Tax Act was amended in December 2013 to remove the relief that had been available up to that time from any obligation to maintain accounting records for a period of at least five years in respect of a company which has been wound up and finally dissolved. The previous relief did not appear to have any effect in relation to companies, since the taxpayer (i.e. the company) that ceases to exist can no longer be held liable, and nothing in the Income Tax Act made any other person responsible for the account records and underlying documentation of the company that has ceased to exist. Since no person was liable, the relief had no application, and the removal of the relief was moot. It remains the case that the Income Tax Act does not make any person responsible for the accounting records and underlying documentation of a company that has ceased to exist.

282. Additionally, section 217 provides that a person is not required to retain any records in respect of which the Collector has notified the person, in writing, that retention is not required (ITA, s. 217). However, the Cook Islands authorities advise that at 2 March 2026 this possibility has never been allowed in practice.

283. For domestic companies that have ceased to exist, in summary, the Income Tax Act does not ensure that accounting records or underlying documentation are available, except to the extent that a profit and loss account is held by the tax authority with annual tax returns. The Companies Act also does not ensure the availability of accounting records or underlying documentation in line with the standard, excepting only if a receiver was engaged in winding up the company. Records will be available if a liquidator was engaged, but this is only ensured for one year and falls short of the period required under the standard. This does not meet the standard.

284. The requirements for domestic and foreign partnerships and trusts upon dissolution relies on the tax law (see paragraph 267-270). In the case of partnerships and trusts that cease to exist or cease to have a nexus with the Cook Islands, the record keeping obligations continue with the relevant partner(s) or trustee(s) that had Cook Islands income tax return obligations.

285. In summary, for domestic companies and foundations, it is not clear who would be legally responsible to keep accounting records and underlying documentation when these entities cease to exist or be registered in the Cook Islands. The Cook Islands is recommended to ensure that accounting records and underlying documentation be kept for at least five years after domestic companies and foundations cease to exist or cease to be registered in the Cook Islands.

Oversight and enforcement of requirements to maintain accounting records

286. The international sector is supervised by the FSC, which has an active and well-structured compliance program that covers each type of company and legal arrangement. Supervision in the domestic sector relies on the Registrar of Companies in the Ministry of Justice, which has conducted minimal compliance activity, and tax audits by the RMD, who have not provided any measures of compliance or demonstrated adequate enforcement processes to enforce compliance.
International sector

287. A director of an international company who fails to take all reasonable steps to secure compliance by the company with the requirements of section 113 commits an offence against the ICA and is liable on conviction to a fine of NZD 1 000 (EUR 504) and to imprisonment for six months (ICA, ss. 113(3) and 219(2)). Failure to comply with any legal obligations imposed by the LLCA is an offence and, on conviction, punishable with a fine not exceeding NZD 10 000 (EUR 5 040) or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or to both (LLCA, s 78).

288. Failure to comply with any legal obligation imposed by the IPA is an offence and, on conviction, punishable by a fine not exceeding NZD 10 000 (EUR 5 040) or imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or both (IPA 1984, s. 79).

289. Failure to comply with any legal obligation imposed by the International Trust Act is an offence and, on conviction, punishable by a fine not exceeding NZD 10 000 (EUR 5 040) or imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or both (ITA, s. 28).

290. The Foundations Act does not impose a penalty for failure to keep the accounting records as required in sections 42 and 43 of the Foundations Act 2012. It was recommended both in the 2015 Report and the 2022 Phase 1 Report that the Cook Islands amend the appropriate legislation to ensure that failure to maintain all accounting records and underlying documentation for at least five years is subject to effective enforcement measures. This remains the case.

291. For international companies and legal arrangements, the supervision lies with the FSC as part of FSC's onsite inspections for trustee companies. Prior to July 2022, all trustee companies had at least one onsite inspection each year, (except for 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic when only the three largest trustee companies were inspected). From July 2022, the cycle time changed based on an assessment of risk and trustee companies have been on a two-year inspection cycle since then. Inspections are primarily onsite and include verifying that the trustee company and/or the client has complied with its obligations to maintain and retain accounting information in respect of its clients and their associated entities.
292. The FSC has provided statistics for its compliance activities during the review period on the types of entities and legal arrangements covered in its inspections.

293. While the relevant laws do not explicitly require limited liability companies, international trusts and foundations to maintain underlying documentation in support of the accounting records (see paragraph 266) in practice the FSC expects these to be available in the inspections. However, transactions are very infrequent as most entities and arrangements are engaged in relatively passive activities such as holding bank account(s), real estate or shares in non-Cook Islands companies. Typically, there are less than five transactions in an annual period and sometimes there are none. The most common transaction found in records is the payment of fees due to the trustee company for their administration services.

294. Issues found in accounting records vary but were considered by the FSC to be relatively minor. These included missing invoices, an unsigned loan agreement, and failures by a trustee company to do a monthly reconciliation to a bank account (by law if the trust company has authority over any bank account it must do monthly reconciliations of activity on those accounts). There have been no prosecutions for failing to keep records. The FSC has issued remedial action plans and recommendations where minor deficiencies have been found during onsite inspections with appropriate follow up.
295. Oversight and enforcement of accounting record obligations in the international sector are appropriate.
Domestic and foreign entities

296. For domestic companies, in case of failure to take all reasonable steps to secure compliance with the record keeping requirements of section 159 of the Companies Act, each director commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding NZD 4 000 (EUR 2 016) or to a term of imprisonment not exceeding three months, or both (CA 2017, s. 158). As described in paragraphs 249 to 251, domestic companies do not file financial statements with the Registrar of Companies, thus accounting records are only required to be kept at the company's registered office or some other place in the Cook Islands. During the review period, the Registrar of Companies carried out little to no activities relevant to ensuring compliance by domestic companies with the company law record keeping obligations. In practice, there is reliance on the RMD to ensure accounting records are maintained under tax law and the RMD is more active in this area.

297. Tax audits carried out during the review period have, in some cases, encompassed the requirements to maintain accounting records and underlying documentation under the tax law. Failure to comply with any obligation established by the Income Tax Act (including failing to keep records) is considered an offence, punished by fines ranging from NZD 1 000 (EUR 504) to NZD 10 000 (EUR 5 040) (Income Tax Act, s. 206).

298. In the case of domestic partnerships and trusts, the same sanction for failing to keep records as mentioned for companies is available for each partner and trustee respectively that is required to file a tax return.

299. During the review period, the RMD conducted 397 tax related audits or reviews (i.e. covering 21% of entities registered in the tax database). Precise statistics are not available, however based on a material sample of case records, the RMD estimates that around a third of all cases test the existence and accuracy of financial statements and half of all cases involve review of underlying documentation (whether or not financial statements were available). No further details of the level of compliance have been provided, except to note that no specific record keeping penalties were imposed for any non-compliance (which is likely due more to the difficulties in imposing sanctions as mentioned in paragraph 101 than there being an absence of non-compliance).

300. Although the RMD has an established tax audit programme for taxpayers known to be active or filing tax returns, there is still a need to ensure compliance with tax return filing for all relevant taxpayers, including identifying those who are active. Assuring compliance with filing by all relevant taxpayers is a prerequisite towards ensuring that financial statements are filed when required and that the scope of active taxpayers required to maintain documentation can be scrutinised. As noted for Element A.1, there are shortcomings in monitoring registrations of taxpayers and ensuring that they file tax returns as required (see paragraphs 101, 194 and 219). It is then also necessary to ensure that record keeping obligations on accounting records that are intended to support the accuracy of those tax returns are enforced. While these matters are covered in many of the tax audits carried out and coverage of taxpayers by these activities is substantial, the Cook Islands has been unable to provide any measures of compliance or demonstrate adequate enforcement processes to enforce compliance. The Cook Islands is recommended to enhance supervision, including the use of enforcement powers, in respect of compliance with the tax law requirements on companies, partnerships and trusts.

301. The Cook Islands received seven requests during the review period where accounting information was in the scope of the request. All requests related to entities and arrangements in the international sector. Six of the requests sought financial statements, bank statements and details of distributions to trust beneficiaries (but no other underlying documentation), and the seventh sought details of distributions to beneficiaries. A.3 Banking Information
Banking information and beneficial ownership information should be available for all account holders.

302. The 2015 Report concluded that the legal and regulatory framework in the Cook Islands requires the availability of banking information to the standard. Identity information on all account-holders and transaction records continues to be made available through anti-money laundering (AML) obligations.

303. Since the 2015 Report, the standard was strengthened in 2016 with an additional requirement of ensuring the availability of beneficial ownership information on all account holders. As discussed in A.1, there were several issues identified with respect to customer due diligence (CDD) requirements under the AML framework as it stood prior to 4 December 2024 which could have affected the availability of beneficial ownership in certain instances. The deficiencies related to identification of beneficial owners of bank accounts were addressed by amendments to the FTRA and its Regulations that came into effect from 4 December 2024. The issue relating to a lack of a specified frequency at which CDD information should be updated existed prior to the amendments and the gap remains. The Cook Islands is recommended to take suitable actions to address the remaining gap in its legal framework.

A.3.1 Record-keeping requirements

305. The Cook Islands has four banks, which are licensed and supervised by the FSC under the provisions of the Banking Act 2011. Three of the banks can be described as domestic banks, whose customers are generally Cook Islands based. One bank may be described as international, as it has a focus on customers with international connections.
Availability of banking information
306. The 2015 Report concluded that Cook Islands' law requires banks to keep records in line with the standard.

307. Banks are subject to the accounting requirements as explained under A.2 and must keep proper accounting records that show and explain their transactions. In addition, under the FTRA, all banks are subject to Anti-Money Laundering (AML) obligations as reporting institutions.

308. As reporting institutions, banks are required to keep records of all transactions for six years from the date the relevant transaction was completed, the end of an ongoing business relationship, or in the absence of any formal end to an ongoing business relationship, the completion of the last transaction in that relationship (FTRA 2017, s. 41(2)). Section 41(1) requires reporting institutions to establish and maintain records including the following information in respect of all transactions:
\- a copy of evidence of identity obtained or produced under CDD, or information that enable a copy to be obtained without significant delay (no longer than five working days)

\- a record of all isolated transactions and transactions carried out in the course of an ongoing business relationship, including identification information, account files, business correspondence records and the results of any analysis undertaken (including risk assessment)

\- such other records that are sufficient to permit the reconstruction of individual transactions and compliance with this Act to a standard that allows a competent authority to investigate and prosecute financial misconduct.

309. In case of a bank insolvency, two alternative courses of action would arise: a court appointed manager may be appointed, or the bank would go into liquidation. Prior to an amendment to the Banking Act in effect from 4 December 2024, the record keeping requirements were therefore transferred to the court-appointed manager or to the liquidator respectively (Banking Act 2011, s. 23). There was no indication on the records retention requirements by a court-appointed manager in the Banking Act. Under company law, a liquidator is only required to maintain the records for a period of at least one year. Therefore, under each of these scenarios the record keeping requirements were insufficient. Section 63 of the Banking Act was amended in December 2024 by adding subsection (3A) which allows the FSC to issue directives upon the winding up of a licensee regarding the retention and access of specified documents to one or more of the following persons for the purpose of ensuring such documents are retained and accessible for a minimum of six years after the completion of the liquidation of a licensee:
• a liquidator or court-appointed manager
• a director or officer of the licensee
• a shareholder of the licensee.

310. The amendment resolves the previous gap. According to the FSC, the amendment to section 63 has codified what was previously established practice. No bank wound up its business in the Cook Islands during the review period. The last occurrence of a bank ceasing business in the Cook Islands was in 2015.
Beneficial ownership information on account holders
311. The standard was strengthened in 2016 to specifically require that beneficial ownership information be available in respect of all account holders.

312. As explained under Element A.1 with regard to the availability of beneficial ownership information for companies under AML law, the FTRA establishes the Cook Islands' AML legal framework. Banks are required, under that framework, to ensure that beneficial ownership information on all of their customers is obtained and verified in accordance with the prescribed CDD measures.

313. A bank, as a reporting institution, must establish, maintain and operate procedures to ensure it conducts CDD before entering into an ongoing business relationship or an isolated transaction with a customer or a person acting on behalf of a customer (FTRA, s. 25). Guidance issued by the FSC confirms that a reporting institution must not proceed with the relationship or transaction if CDD cannot be completed. The retention period is six years from end of relationship or one-off transaction (FTRA 2017, s. 44).

314. A reporting institution may rely on a third party to undertake the CDD required under AML law. The third party must be an AML-obliged person and compliant with Financial Action Task Force regulations (FTRA 2017, s. 34(1)). If a reporting institution relies on a third party to undertake CDD, it must: (i) document the basis for its satisfaction that the requirements $^{30}$ to rely on third party information have been met except where the third party is a licensed financial institution, and (ii) obtain the necessary information required for the relevant level of CDD before it enters into the ongoing business relationship or isolated transaction, and (iii) ensure that copies of necessary information obtained in relation to the customer will be made available to it from the third party upon request without delay (FTRA 2017, s. 34(3)). The reporting institution relying on the third party to conduct CDD, and not the third party, is responsible for ensuring that CDD is carried out in compliance with the requirements of the FTRA 2017. The requirements when a reporting institution can rely on a third party's performance of the CDD is in line with the standard. In practice, none of the four banks licensed in the Cook Islands use or accept CDD conducted by a third party.

315. Reporting institutions may undertake simplified CDD procedures. The main distinction with the standard CDD procedure is that under the simplified CDD there is no requirement to verify the identity of the ultimate principal. Simplified CDD procedures may be undertaken by reporting institutions when: (i) they are sure that there are no circumstances preventing them to do so (e.g. the case falls under the enhanced CDD or the customer is a legal arrangement for holding personal assets); (ii) the level of risk associated with the person(s) is low; and (iii) they obtain information on the nature and intended purpose of the ongoing business relationship or isolated transaction (FTRA, s. 27(2)). Further, a reporting institution may undertake simplified CDD on a legal person whose securities are listed on a recognised stock exchange or any other person that may be prescribed (FTRA, s. 27(4)). No other persons have been prescribed.

$^{30}$ A reporting institution may rely on a third party to undertake CDD procedures if the following requirements are met: a) the reporting institution is satisfied that the third party it intends to rely upon is subject to and supervised for compliance with combating money laundering, financing of terrorism and proliferation of weapons of mass destruction consistent with the standards set by the FATF and has adequate measures in place to comply with those requirements; b) the reporting institution takes appropriate steps to identify, assess and understand the financial misconduct risks particular to the jurisdictions that the third party operates in; and c) the third party is able and willing to provide, without delay, upon the reporting institution's request any data, documents or information obtained by the third party with respect to the measures applied on the reporting institution's customer, which the reporting institution would be required or would want to obtain (FTRA, s. 34(2)).

316. The 2022 Report identified three issues with respect to CDD in the AML framework, which had the potential to affect the availability of beneficial ownership during the review period. First, it was not clear whether the concept of ultimate principal should be interpreted as meaning any person who controls the company acting directly or indirectly and acting individually or jointly. This was addressed by amendments to the FTRA which have been analysed under Element A.1. Second, there was no requirement to identify a person holding a senior managerial position when no individual meets the definition of beneficial owner. This was also addressed by amendments to the FTRA which have been analysed under Element A.1. Third, it was noted that reporting institutions are not explicitly required to identify the beneficial owner of a bank account held by a natural person. However, the FTRA defines a customer to include any person on whose behalf the account or transaction is being conducted, and this would therefore require the reporting institution to conduct due diligence on such a person and not confine its attention only to the person who is nominally the account holder. Other provisions in the FTRA support this requirement, including requirements to take reasonable measures to identify the source of funds, and on an ongoing basis apply appropriate scrutiny over transactions to ensure that they are consistent with the reporting institution's knowledge of the customer, its business and level of risk, and where appropriate the source of funds. It is also an offence for a person to deal with a reporting financial institution in a way that avoids the requirements of the Act to identify and verify the identity of another person. A reporting institution that has reasonable grounds to suspect that a person has failed to disclose their status as a nominee must conduct enhanced due diligence (FTRA, s. 56). Overall, it is considered that these collective requirements oblige a reporting institution to take measures to identify when a nominal customer is acting on behalf of another person and if so, conduct CDD on that other person.

317. Reporting institutions are required to carry out ongoing and effective monitoring of any ongoing business relationship, including review of information held for the purpose of customer due diligence to ensure that it is up to date and appropriate (FTRA, s. 32(2)). However, there is no guidance in the FTRA on the frequency of updates of the beneficial ownership information. The actual practices of the banks are described in paragraph 145, which are based on their own policies and not based on any frequency specified in the AML framework. The Cook Islands is recommended to ensure that information on beneficial owners of bank account holders is up to date in line with the standard.
Oversight and enforcement

318. The FSC and FIU conduct joint inspections to monitor compliance of banks with all relevant obligations. Banks must establish and maintain a register that contains a copy of every report submitted to the FIU and all related records. A reporting institution must keep the reports for a period of six years after the date on which the report or the enquiry is made (FTRA 2017, s. 43).

319. Failure to comply with the FTRA obligations is considered an offence and punishable by: (i) in the case of an individual, a fine of up to NZD 250 000 (EUR 126 000) or imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or both; (ii) in any other case, a fine of up to NZD 1 000 000 (EUR 504 000) (FTRA 2017, s. 63).

320. The FSC and FIU have a long-standing practice of conducting inspections of every bank annually and this continued throughout the review period. The reviews also continue to be conducted in the manner described in paragraphs 241 and 242 of the 2015 Report and it remains the case that the results indicate a high rate of compliance.

322. Sections B.1 and B.2 evaluate whether competent authorities have the power to obtain and provide information that is the subject of a request under an EOI arrangement from any person within their territorial jurisdiction who is in possession or control of such information, and whether rights and safeguards are compatible with effective EOI.
B.1 Competent authority's ability to obtain and provide information

Competent authorities should have the power to obtain and provide information that is the subject of a request under an exchange of information arrangement from any person within their territorial jurisdiction who is in possession or control of such information (irrespective of any legal obligation on such person to maintain the secrecy of the information).

323. The 2015 Report concluded that the Competent Authority in the Cook Islands has broad access powers to obtain all types of relevant information, including ownership, accounting and banking information from any person, in order to comply with obligations under Cook Islands' EOI instruments. These access powers can be used regardless of domestic tax interest in the requested information. In case of failure on the part of the information holder to provide the requested information, the Competent Authority has adequate powers to compel the production of information. Finally, secrecy provisions contained in Cook Islands' law are compatible with effective exchange of information.

324. The ability of the Revenue Management Division to obtain information for exchange of information purposes derives from its general access powers under sections 86 and 219 to 222 of the Income Tax Act coupled with the authority provided by the relevant exchange of information agreements. In 2016, sections 219 and 220 were amended to extend the access powers in order to facilitate compliance by the Cook Islands with its obligations to automatically exchange financial account information. In 2017, the Income Tax Act was amended to enhance access to electronic storage media with an obligation to provide reasonable assistance and any basis for authentication and decryption.

325. During the review period, the Cook Islands received seven requests for information (including ownership, accounting and banking information) and the Competent Authority has successfully used its access powers to obtain this information. However, while no issues with access powers have arisen for EOI due to information holders so far always being cooperative, the RMD has not shown a willingness or readiness to escalate its actions to compel the provision of information when there has been a failure to cooperate with information requests for domestic purposes. This is indicative of a risk that the current administrative framework and practice could affect the exercise of access powers to obtain information for EOI purposes in the future.

text: B.1.1 Ownership, identity and banking information and B.1.2 Accounting records

327. The competent authority designated under the Cook Islands' EOI agreements is the Collector of Inland Revenue who belongs to the Revenue Management Division (RMD), or an authorised representative of the Collector.
328. Subsection 219(1) of the Income Tax Amendment Act 2011 sets out the Competent Authority's access powers as follows:

Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other Act, including without limitation Sections 227 and 249 of the International Companies Act 1981-82, Section 23 of the International Trusts Act 1984, the Foundations Act 2012, the Captive Insurance Act 2013 and Section 72 of the Limited Liability Companies Act 2008, the Collector or any officer of the Department authorised in that behalf shall at all times have full and free access to records for the purpose of inspecting such books or documents, whether in the custody or under the control of a public officer or a body corporate or any other person, for the purposes of inspecting any records which the Collector or the officer of the Department considers necessary, relevant, or likely to provide information, for the purposes of (a) collecting any tax or duty which the Collector is authorised to collect; (b) giving effect to agreements described in [section 86] $^{31}$ or giving effect to Part VIA. $^{32}$

329. This subsection ensures that the Competent Authority has access powers in respect of any information held by “a public officer or a body corporate or any other person” who is believed to be in possession or control of that information. The powers apply whether or not the information is required to be kept pursuant to an explicit legal obligation. Also, the power to obtain information extends to any person and any third parties, such as accounting firms. This is expressly provided under section 220(1) of the Income Tax Act which further enhances section 219:

Every person (including any officer employed in or in connection with any department of the Government or by any public authority, and any other public officer) shall, if required by the Collector or by any officer of the

$^{31}$ In the Income Tax (Automatic Exchange of Financial Account Information and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2016, the reference is made to section 186. The Cook Islands confirmed that section 86 is the placement reference that should be used in the 2016 Amendment Act and communicated this drafting error to competent authorities.

$^{32}$ Section 86 authorises the entry into international agreements for relief from double taxation and the exchange of information, i.e. DTCs. Part VIA refers to the “Implementation of arrangements to exchange tax information or provide other mutual assistance in tax matters” and thus covers bilateral TIEAs, the Multilateral Convention and the Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement on Automatic Exchange of Financial Account Information.

330. Section 220(1) was amended in 2017 by inserting the following subsections:

(1A) If a person fails to furnish information or produce records as required under subsection 1, the Collector or an authorised officer may seize any electronic information storage media on which the information or records are stored and retain the media for as long as is necessary to copy the information or records.

(1B) A person whose electronic information storage media has been seized under subsection 1A must provide reasonable assistance to enable the Collector or authorised officer to access the information or records stored on the media, including the entering of the password or other basis of authentication for access to the media, or providing decryption information necessary to decrypt data on the media.

331. Storage media was extended to include portable devices such as computers, phones, cameras and storage media and other facilities such as cloud storage (Income Tax Amendment Act 2017, ss. 22 to 24).

332. Section 220(2) of the ITA further provides that “information in writing which may be required under this section shall include lists of shareholders of companies, with the amount of capital contributed by and dividends paid to each shareholder, copies of balance sheets and of profit and loss accounts, and other accounts and statements of assets and liabilities of any person”.
333. The ITA provides the Collector with comprehensive information gathering powers. They are very wide and not limited to persons who are required to maintain this information.
Accessing information generally

334. After receiving a valid EOI request, the process for accessing information is as follows. The Collector or his/her authorised representative determines whether the information is already in the possession of the RMD by accessing RMD records, which could be the case for individuals, domestic companies and domestic trusts if subject to Cook Islands tax, but is not likely to be the case for international companies and trusts and limited liability companies or persons related to them, which are more frequently the subject of EOI requests from partners. If the information is not already in the possession of the RMD, an official request for information under section 220 of the Income Tax Act is issued. The RMD has a template it uses for this purpose, which states that the information request is pursuant to section 220 of the Income Tax Act. The request may be done electronically (Income Tax Amendment Act 2017, s. 26). A response is usually due within 14 days from the day after the date of the RMD request (being the allotted time for the requested party to challenge the request in the High Court) and a reminder is set for the due date for the response.

335. With respect to domestic companies, the RMD may also use its access powers to obtain information from the Ministry of Justice (Registrar of Companies) on where ownership information is maintained (see paragraph 5855). As the Ministry is located a short walk from the RMD, and the relevant staff and their authorities are well known to one another, this is actioned by way of instant on-site request under section 220, which does not require a notice in writing.

336. Having due regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, the Collector issues requests to the persons most likely to have this information under their possession or control. Depending on the nature of the request, the information may be held by the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) or by the trustee company acting for an international entity or arrangement (for instance ownership and identity information). In the latter case, the FSC provides the RMD with the identity of the relevant trustee company if not already known to the RMD. Once the relevant trustee company has been identified, a new official notice for information under section 220 is issued by the RMD to the trustee company.

337. Up until 2022, the notice identified that it was being made under an international agreement and named the agreement. The procedure changed from 2023 so that the default practice is that the request does not give any indication of an EOI purpose and states only that information is being requested pursuant to the general power in section 220 of the Income Tax Act. There is an exception to this generic approach, if the request is for information or documents that would only be relevant to prior years beyond the standard domestic statutory limitation on amending tax returns, which is four years from the end of the year in which an assessment was made. There was one such case in the review period. In this case, it was considered necessary, in order to demonstrate that the power is being exercised lawfully, to identify that it was made under the relevant agreement and not for a domestic purpose subject to a shorter timeframe. While the preference would be to only name the Multilateral Convention without naming the jurisdiction, in the particular case in question the request was made under a TIEA and that TIEA was named (consequently also including the name of the jurisdiction). As the exception is limited to circumstances where it is necessary to exercise the power, it is in line with the standard.
Accessing identity, legal and beneficial ownership information

338. Information held by the Registrar of domestic companies relating to legal ownership may be made available to the Collector through use of the general access powers described above. The Collector may also use the general powers to access the legal and beneficial ownership information held by the company itself and service providers that are AML-obliged persons.

339. In the case of international companies, trusts and limited liability companies, legal and beneficial ownership must be held by trustee companies who are AML-obliged persons and the same general access powers are applicable in the same manner. The AML secrecy provisions in Cook Islands legislation are overridden by the access powers in the Income Tax Act (ss. 219 and 220), which are explicitly stated to apply despite anything to the contrary in any other Act, and furthermore are also stated to be available for the purposes of giving effect to any international agreements under section 86. Therefore, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the AML legislation, the RMD must have access for the purposes of collecting any tax or giving effect to EOIR agreements.

340. The scope of all seven requests in the review period included trusts believed to be Cook Islands international trusts, either identifying the trusts or identifying individuals with a request for information on the trusts potentially related to the individuals. Therefore, all seven requests required checks for the existence of identity, legal and beneficial information, although such information could not always be provided when connections were not found. When obtaining identity, legal and beneficial ownership information during the review period, the RMD relied on the trustee companies, who provided information promptly. In the case of a series of three requests from an exchange partner, the partner named a trust suspected of potentially being a Cook Islands international trust, with the later two requests naming additional individuals suspected to be connected to that trust. When the FSC was unable to identify any such trust in the trust register or that the individuals were connected to any Cook Islands trust, the RMD took the further step of conducting a secondary check with the banks who also provided information promptly (confirming no client relationships with the trust or the individuals). The partner was advised of the outcome of these investigations and has raised no concerns.
Accessing banking and accounting information

341. The powers of the Collector are also sufficient to effectively access banking and accounting information. The Cook Islands authorities added that they can access information even if only the bank account number is known to the requesting jurisdiction, or only a name is provided. If the EOI request has not identified a specific bank, a notice would generally be sent to all four banks. However, if the contextual information behind the request indicates that the international bank is the most likely bank with relevant information, a request may be sent to that bank first and further requests to the three domestic banks might only be sent if the first request obtains no result.

342. Five requests were received for banking information during the period. In practice, Cook Islands' banks are very responsive to requests from the RMD and provided information within the requested timeframe, which is 7 to 21 days depending on the circumstances.
343. Seven requests included accounting information within the scope of the request, and the information was obtained from trustee companies in a timely manner.
B.1.3 Use of information gathering measures absent domestic tax interest

344. The concept of “domestic tax interest” describes a situation where a contracting party can only provide information to another contracting party if it has an interest in the requested information for its tax purposes. The standard requires a jurisdiction to be able to use its information gathering powers, notwithstanding that it may not need the information for its tax purposes.

345. The Cook Islands has no domestic tax interest limitation with respect to its information gathering powers. The broad access powers provided to the Collector can be used to obtain and provide information for the express purpose of giving effect to Cook Islands' EOI agreements (Income Tax Act, ss. 86, 219 and 220). In practice, the Cook Islands successfully used its access powers during the review period to obtain information on or relevant to individuals, entities and legal arrangements where there was no domestic tax interest.
B.1.4 Effective enforcement provisions to compel the production of information

346. The Cook Islands has enforcement provisions, including monetary penalties and search and seizure powers, to compel the production of information (refer to the 2015 Report, paragraphs 264 to 268).

347. The Collector has the authority to enter premises without going through any special process, except for private premises (Income Tax Act, s. 219(1B)). Private premises may only be entered with the consent of the occupier or pursuant to a warrant. A Judge of the High Court is authorised to provide the Collector with an access warrant, on written application made under oath, if the judge is satisfied that the Collector's request is valid (Income Tax Act, s. 219(3)).

348. The Collector may also apply to a Judge of the High Court for the Court to hold an inquiry for the purpose of obtaining any information required for the purposes of administering or enforcing the Income Tax Act, including giving effect to international agreements (Income Tax Act, s. 221). If such an inquiry is approved, the Judge may summon and examine under oath any relevant person. The Judge has jurisdiction and authority over a witness as it would under a civil action in its ordinary jurisdiction, and a summoned witness has the same rights and liabilities as they would in such a civil action.

349. In 2017, the penalty for failure to provide information for EOI purposes on request of the Collector was increased from NZD 1 000 (EUR 504) to NZD 10 000 (EUR 5 040). Under section 206 of the Income Tax Act, this fine is imposed on every person who commits one of the following offences:
\- refuses or fails to furnish any return or information as and when required by this Act, or any regulation made under this Act, or by the Collector
\- wilfully or negligently makes any false return, or gives false information, or misleads or attempts to mislead the Collector or any other liability to taxation
\- refuses or fails without lawful jurisdiction to duly attend and give evidence to the person, or to produce any book or paper required
\- obstructs any officer acting in the discharge of the officer's duties or in the exercise of the officer's powers under this Act

• commits any other breach of this Act for which no other penalty is expressly provided or
\- aids, abets, or incites any other person to commit any offence against this Act or against any regulation made under this Act.

350. In addition, every person who commits an offence in relation to sections 219 to 222 of the Income Tax Act, for which no other penalty is prescribed, is liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding NZD 10 000 (EUR 5 040) (Income Tax Act, s. 223, Income Tax Amendment Act 2017, s. 25). An Amendment to the Income Tax Act (Automatic Exchange of Financial Account Information and Other Matters) in 2016 further introduced the penalties for non-compliance with the regulations under specific Part VIA on the “Implementation of arrangements to exchange tax information or provide other mutual assistance in tax matters” as fines not exceeding NZD 10 000 (EUR 5 040) for an individual and not exceeding NZD 100 000 (EUR 50 400) for a body corporate (Income Tax (Automatic Exchange of Financial Account Information and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2016, s. 6).

351. A certificate in writing signed by the Collector certifying that a person refused or failed to furnish any return or information as and when required by the Act or by the Collector will, in the absence of proof to the contrary, be accepted as sufficient evidence in any proceedings against this person (Income Tax Act, s. 206(3)). All proceedings for offences against the Income Tax Act must be taken by way of prosecution in the High Court (Income Tax Act, s. 207).

352. During the review period, there were no EOI cases where an information holder failed to cooperate with a request for information in relation to EOI requests. No escalated action, such as prosecution or engagement with the Court, occurred, whether for EOI or domestic access purposes and no records of such action are known to exist for any years since the Income Tax Act was enacted in 1997. The usual information sources for EOI requests are government authorities and a small pool of financial institutions and trustee companies who have a long history of cooperation with the RMD. As a small jurisdiction that also has a small taxpayer base, its taxpayers are generally found to be cooperative when access powers are used for domestic purposes, so that the RMD has largely had no cause to escalate enforcement action to obtain information. However, one recent instance of the exercise of access powers for domestic purposes raises a potential concern over practice.

353. In October 2023, a request was made for information for domestic purposes, which only received a partial response. Two reminders were issued, followed by a further formal notice in November 2023 under section 220 of the Income Tax Act. No response was received to this notice, so a letter advising breach was issued in January 2024. No further action has been taken with the taxpayer. Instead, the RMD opted to pursue the information through a request to a partner jurisdiction with which the Cook Islands taxpayer had connections including to relevant related parties (also see Element C.5.2 in relation to this outgoing request, paragraph 437). The absence of any administrative penalty in the legal framework and the necessity to go to court in the Cook Islands to prosecute or to otherwise obtain judicial assistance have been cited as practical factors in the decision made, including not having an in-house legal practitioner in the RMD to engage with the court. While this case was exceptional and did not relate to an inward EOI request, and EOI related information sources have a history of being cooperative, there are a range of other types of relatively common non-compliance with tax obligations in the Cook Islands that can only be sanctioned by prosecution in court and the same administrative impediments have meant that in practice the RMD has not prosecuted any taxpayer for many years. There is therefore a clear risk that the current administrative framework and practice could affect the exercise of access powers to obtain information for EOI purposes in the future, in case of non-cooperation of an information holder. The Cook Islands is recommended to ensure that appropriate enforcement actions, including sanctions, are taken in cases of non-compliance or delays by information holders.

B.1.5 Secrecy provisions

354. The 2015 Report found that there were no secrecy provisions which would prevent the Cook Islands' Competent Authority from obtaining information (refer to paragraph 269). There are various secrecy provisions in Cook Islands legislation, $^{33}$ but these are overridden by the Income Tax Act (ss. 86, 219 and 220). The Income Tax Amendment Act 2011 specifically overrides any obligation to secrecy that may be imposed by any other Act (Income Tax Act, s. 86(5)). There have been no material changes to the relevant legal framework since that report.
Bank secrecy

355. Under the Banking Act 2011, “no person shall disclose information relating to the banking business of a licensee or of a depositor or other customer of the licensee” (Banking Act, s. 54). However, exceptions apply. In particular, disclosure is permitted for the purpose of discharging any duty, performing any function or exercising any power under the Banking Act or any other act (Banking Act, s. 54(2)(b)). Therefore, banking secrecy is no impediment to access powers of the Competent Authority.

356. No issues were raised by peers in connection with bank secrecy and neither the banking representatives nor the Cook Islands authorities met at the onsite visit identified any issues in practice. Banks provided information in all cases requested.
Professional secrecy

357. Attorney-client privilege exists in the Cook Islands under the Code of Ethics set out in the Schedule to the Law Practitioners Act 1993-94. Section 6 provides that “any oral or written communication between practitioners shall be accorded confidentiality, unless agreed otherwise by a client, or as may be required by law”. Furthermore, section 18 establishes that “a practitioner should never disclose, unless lawfully ordered to do so by the Court or as required by law, what has been communicated to him in his capacity as a practitioner, even after he has ceased to be the client’s counsel. This duty extends to his partners, to practitioners assisting him and to his employees”. (emphasis added).

358. As found in the 2015 Report, the scope of these restrictions is in line with the standard. Privilege is not an impediment to the exercise of access powers of the Competent Authority, particularly given the combined effect of the Income Tax Act and the Cook Islands' TIEAs and the Multilateral Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters, whereby the Income Tax Act overrides legal privilege, but only so far as is necessary for the Cook Islands to meet its obligations under these international agreements (Income Tax Act, s. 86(1)). The limits on information which must be exchanged under the Cook Islands' TIEAs mirror those provided for in the OECD Model TIEA and the Multilateral Convention. Accordingly, communications between a client and an attorney or other admitted legal representative are only privileged to the extent that the attorney or other legal representative acts in his or her capacity as an attorney or other legal representative. Therefore, the attorney-client privilege in the Cook Islands is no impediment to access powers of the Competent Authority.

359. In practice, it was not necessary for the Cook Islands Competent Authority to rely on legal professionals or accountants as a source of information for EOI purposes during the review period. The RMD has no record of ever using legal professionals as an information source, neither for EOI or for domestic purposes. Given this historical lack of relevance as information sources, specialist legal practitioners did not attend the onsite visit, however some of the trustee company personnel are from the legal profession and the trustee companies expressed no divergence in views from the RMD on the application of legal privilege described above. In any case, no claims for any legal privilege were made by trustee companies during the review period and there was no recollection of any such claims ever being made in the past.
