B.2 Notification requirements, rights and safeguards
The rights and safeguards (e.g. notification, appeal rights) that apply to persons in the requested jurisdiction should be compatible with effective exchange of information.

360. The 2015 Report found that there were no issues regarding prior notification requirements or appeal rights. The legal framework was determined to be in place and its implementation Compliant with the standard. This continues to be the case.
361. The conclusions are as follows:
Legal and regulatory framework: In place
The rights and safeguards that apply to persons in the Cook Islands are compatible with effective exchange of information.
Practical implementation of the standard: Compliant
The application of the rights and safeguards in the Cook Islands is compatible with effective exchange of information.
B.2.1 Rights and safeguards should not unduly prevent or delay effective exchange of information
Notification of the information holder

362. There are no general legal requirements for the Cook Islands' RMD to inform a person subject to a request for information of the existence of the exchange of information request prior to or after exchange. Likewise, the RMD is not obliged to inform the taxpayer concerned prior to or after contacting third parties to obtain information.
363. In practice, where information is held by another government authority (such as the Financial Supervisory Commission), the taxpayer would not be notified.

364. For all information holders, including non-government information holders, since 2022 the notices to provide information generally only quote the access power being used under the Income Tax Act, which is the same power as is applicable to obtain information for domestic purposes (but see paragraph 337 for the single exception). When, as is usual, no EOI agreement is mentioned, there are no other details in the notice that would directly lead the recipient to conclude that the notice is for EOI purposes. However, the RMD understands that trustee companies would nevertheless usually intuit that a notice is highly likely to be for EOI purposes as their clients are not generally of interest to the RMD for domestic tax purposes. Whether this intuition always leads to the trustee company informing the client is not known, however the RMD understands that they would usually inform their client, and no law prevents them from doing so. The RMD also understands that practices are different with the banks, with each of the four banks confirming that they do not inform the client when notices for information are received from the RMD.

365. None of the requests for information received by the Cook Islands in the review period asked that the Cook Islands refrain from notifying the taxpayer. In the event that a partner did include this request in the future and the information needed to be obtained from a trustee company, the Cook Islands Competent Authority advises that it would communicate with the requesting jurisdiction explaining the circumstances above and ask whether it still wished to proceed with the request in the circumstances. The requirement for RMD staff to do this is included in the EOI Manual.
Appeal rights

366. If a person or a public authority who receives a notice from the Collector believes that the notice is improper, he/she may apply to the High Court to have the notice discharged or varied within 14 days from the date of receipt (Income Tax Act, s. 220(4)). A notice may be considered to be improper where the Collector does not have a legal basis for obtaining the information, for example because the notice for information is not in conformity with the terms of a relevant international agreement (but see paragraphs 336 and 362 on whether the person would know or suspect that a notice was made under such terms).

367. On hearing such application, the Court may discharge the notice or make such variation to it as it thinks fit. If the Court decides that the notice is proper, the person or public authority may not appeal this decision. In practice, no appeal has ever taken place in relation to any notice, whether for domestic or EOI purposes.
368. The rights and safeguards (e.g. notification, appeal rights) that apply to persons in the Cook Islands are compatible with the requirement to ensure effective exchange of information.

369. Sections C.1 to C.5 evaluate the effectiveness of the Cook Islands' network of EOI mechanisms – whether these EOI mechanisms provide for exchange of the right scope of information, cover all of the Cook Islands' relevant partners, whether there were adequate provisions to ensure the confidentiality of information received, whether the Cook Islands' network of EOI mechanisms respects the rights and safeguards of taxpayers and whether the Cook Islands can provide the information requested in an effective manner.
C.1 Exchange of information mechanisms
Exchange of information mechanisms should provide for effective exchange of information.

370. The 2015 Report identified that the Cook Islands has a network of EOI agreements that allow for EOI on request in accordance with the international standard, resulting in a determination of the legal framework as “in place” and rated as Compliant.

371. In 2015, the Cook Islands' EOI network covered 17 jurisdictions. The Cook Islands signed the Multilateral Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters (the Multilateral Convention) on 28 October 2016, which entered into force on 1 September 2017. The EOI network now covers 151 jurisdictions through the Multilateral Convention and 20 TIEAs (i.e. 3 new TIEAs compared to the 2015 Report, with Belgium, Canada and the Czech Republic; see Annex 2). All TIEA partners are also covered by the Multilateral Convention, therefore all EOI relationships of the Cook Islands meet the standard.
372. The Cook Islands legal framework does not present any issue that would compromise the effective exchange of information or otherwise frustrate the application of these EOI mechanisms.

373. The legal basis on which EOI requests took place between the Cook Islands and partners over the review period was a Tax Information Exchange Agreement (TIEA) for one partner and the Multilateral Convention for three partners.
374. The conclusions are as follows:
Legal and regulatory framework: In place
No material deficiencies have been identified in the EOI mechanisms of the Cook Islands.
Practical implementation of the standard: Compliant
No issues have been identified that would affect EOIR in practice.

Other forms of exchange of information

375. In addition to exchange of information on request, the Cook Islands is also involved in automatic exchange of financial account information. The first non-reciprocal exchanges took place in September 2018 and reciprocal exchanges started as from 2019. There is no use of spontaneous exchanges.
C.1.1 Standard of foreseeable relevance

376. The 2015 Report concluded the Cook Islands' TIEAs allowed for exchange of information in accordance with the standard of foreseeable relevance. This is also the case for the three TIEAs signed since that report, as well as for the Multilateral Convention.
Clarifications and foreseeable relevance in practice

377. The peer input received for the current review did not raise any concerns with the Cook Islands' interpretation or practices with foreseeable relevance of requests made by peers. The Cook Islands confirmed that the RMD verifies all information to establish the foreseeable relevance of incoming and outgoing requests. There is a manual giving guidance by referring to Article 26 of the Model Taxation Convention and its Commentary on fishing and foreseeable relevance. The Cook Islands require incoming EOI requests to include background information, including an explanation of the tax purpose for which the information is requested, the type of investigations carried out by the requesting authority and a description of the efforts made by the requesting jurisdiction to obtain the information domestically. The Cook Islands sought clarification on three requests received during the review period, specifically in an effort to identify whether a trust was a Cook Islands trust, ultimately determining and communicating to the partner that the trust had no connection to the Cook Islands.
Group requests

378. The Cook Islands' EOI agreements and domestic law do not contain language prohibiting group requests. The EOI Manual of the Cook Islands interprets them as allowing the provision of information requested pursuant to group requests and refers to Article 26 of the Model Taxation Convention and its commentaries.

379. The Cook Islands did not receive any group requests during the period under review. The EOI Manual includes a section on the “Foreseeable Relevance of Group Requests”. This section explains that the standard of foreseeable relevance can be met in respect of a group of taxpayers that are not individually identified, if the requesting jurisdiction provides: (i) a detailed description of the group and the facts and circumstances that led to the request, (ii) an explanation of the applicable law and why there is reason to believe that the taxpayers in the group have been non-compliant with that law, and (iii) an explanation of how the requested information would assist in determining compliance by the taxpayers in the group. The EOI Manual also usefully explains that a third party could have contributed to the non-compliance of the taxpayers in the group. This procedure is aligned to the OECD Commentary to Model Article 26. EOI staff demonstrated awareness of the concepts and would be expected to refresh their understanding through reference to the Manual in the event that a group request is received. The Cook Islands made three group requests in the review period, which were accepted and actioned by the partner, demonstrating familiarity in the Cook Islands with the requirements of group requests.
C.1.2 Provide for exchange of information in respect of all persons

380. All TIEAs signed by the Cook Islands contain a provision concerning jurisdictional scope which is equivalent to Article 2 of the OECD Model TIEA and which conforms to the international standard. The Multilateral Convention also allows for exchange of information in respect of all persons.

381. The Cook Islands states that it did not receive any request for information during the review period with respect to persons who were not residents either of the Cook Islands or the requesting jurisdiction. The Cook Islands EOI Manual states that foreseeably relevant covers information in respect of all persons and is not limited to persons resident in the jurisdiction. No peers raised issues on this subject.
C.1.3 Obligation to exchange all types of information

382. All TIEAs signed by the Cook Islands contain a provision similar to Article 5(4) of the OECD Model TIEA, which ensures that the requested jurisdiction shall not decline to supply the information requested solely because it is held by a financial institution, nominee or person acting in an agency or a fiduciary capacity, or because it relates to ownership interests in a person. The Multilateral Convention also foresees the obligation to exchange all types of information.

383. Over the review period, the Cook Islands exchanged multiple types of information, including legal and beneficial ownership, banking and accounting information. It did not decline any requests for any reason. The EOI Manual does not provide for declining a request for any reason that would be inconsistent with its obligation to exchange all types of information. Peers did not raise any concerns in this regard in the inputs provided.
C.1.4 Absence of domestic tax interest

384. The concept of “domestic tax interest” describes a situation where a contracting party can only provide information to another contracting party if it has an interest in the requested information for its own tax purposes. An inability to provide information based on a domestic tax interest requirement is not consistent with the standard.

385. All TIEAs concluded by the Cook Islands contain a provision similar to Article 5(2) of the OECD Model TIEA, which allows information to be obtained and exchanged notwithstanding it is not required for a domestic tax purpose. The Multilateral Convention also allows for exchange of information regardless of a domestic tax interest.

386. Commonly, EOI requests received by the Cook Islands relate to information with which it has no domestic tax interest, and this was the case for all seven requests received in the review period. The Cook Islands provided responses in all cases and peers did not raise any concerns in this regard in the inputs provided.
C.1.5 and C.1.6 Civil and criminal tax matters

387. The Cook Islands' network of agreements provides for exchange in both civil and criminal matters, with no dual criminality restriction. In practice, four of the requests received in the review period related to criminal tax matters and these were accepted and actioned by the Cook Islands without regard to any dual criminality condition.
C.1.7 Provide information in specific form requested
388. The Cook Islands' agreements have no restrictions that would prevent it from providing information in a specific form.

389. The Collector has not been requested to provide information in a particular form during the review period but does not foresee difficulties in providing information in a requested form, for example as a sworn affidavit.

C.3 Confidentiality
The jurisdiction's information exchange mechanisms should have adequate provisions to ensure the confidentiality of information received.
395. The 2015 Report concluded that the confidentiality provisions in the Cook Islands' EOI instruments and domestic laws were in line with the standard. This continues to be the case.
396. The Cook Islands has policies and organisational procedures that ensure the compliance with confidentiality requirements in practice.
397. The conclusions are as follows:
Legal and regulatory framework: In place
No material deficiencies have been identified in the EOI mechanisms and legislation of the Cook Islands concerning confidentiality of information received.
Practical implementation of the standard: Compliant
No material deficiencies have been identified and the confidentiality of information exchange is effective.
C.3.1 Information received: disclosure, use and safeguards

398. All of the Cook Islands' EOI instruments have secrecy provisions ensuring the confidentiality of information exchanged and limiting the disclosure and use of information received. In addition, section 86(1) of the Income Tax Act, as amended, provides that EOI provisions have effect “according to their tenor” notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any enactment. This means that the provisions pertaining to confidentiality of information form part of the body of Cook Islands domestic law. The Income Tax Act expressly provides that the above secrecy provisions shall not prevent the Collector from disclosing such information “as is required to be disclosed” under EOIR instruments (Income Tax Act, s. 86(5)).

399. The confidentiality provisions of the Cook Islands' EOIR instruments are backed up by the general secrecy provisions in section 7 of the Income Tax Act: The Collector and every officer shall not communicate any matters relating to the Income Tax Act to any person, except for the purpose of giving effect to this Act or any other enactment imposing taxes or duties payable to the Crown. In 2017, an Income Tax Amendment Act was introduced to enhance the secrecy provisions to expressly prevent the unauthorised disclosure of information held under EOI instruments with other jurisdictions and increase penalty for contravening the secrecy provision from NZD 500 (EUR 252) to NZD 5 000 (EUR 2 520) (Income Tax Amendment Act 2017, s. 5). A prison sentence of not more than six months can also be imposed in accordance with the same provision in case of breach of confidentiality. The Cook Islands confirmed that the secrecy provisions continue to apply after the cessation of employment.

400. The Cook Islands has an Official Information Act 2008 $^{34}$ that allows the disclosure of the communications between jurisdictions to persons who request for such disclosure, unless disclosure would prejudice the entrusting of information to the Government of Cook Islands on a basis of confidence by the government of any other country or an agency of such a government or by any international organisation (Official Information Act, s. 6). The Cook Islands authorities have never received a request for disclosure of information received pursuant to a TIEA or the Multilateral Convention but are confident that the exception of section 6 would apply. In addition, section 7 of the Income Tax Act specifies that information can be communicated only for the purpose of giving effect to this Act or any other enactment imposing taxes or duties payable to the Crown. The Official Information Act does not impose taxes or duties payable to the Crown. In practice, freedom of information requests received in the domestic tax context have been refused where appropriate, including where a request was not made in good faith.

$^{34}$ Under section 5 of the Official Information Act 2008, a person has rights to access information relating to himself unless there is a good reason to withhold it under section 6.

401. The Terms of Reference, as amended in 2016, clarified that although it remains the rule that information exchanged cannot be used for purposes other than tax purposes, an exception applies where the EOI agreement provides that the information may be used for such other purposes under the laws of both contracting parties and the competent authority supplying the information authorises the use of information for purposes other than tax purposes. The Cook Islands' Competent Authority is restricted from granting authorisation to use the information for other purposes, also when a requesting partner seeks the Cook Islands' consent, by the section 7 of the Official Information Act 2008 maintaining secrecy provisions which has effect on the Competent Authorities' ability to authorise requests for non-tax purposes. In general, use of information for non-tax purposes is not permitted in the Cook Islands pursuant to section 7(1) of the Income Tax Act 1997. There are no other domestic legal provisions giving effect to use of information for non-tax purposes. In practice, the Cook Islands reported that over the review period no requesting partner sought the Cook Islands' consent to utilise the information for non-tax purposes. One request of this nature was made by a partner in an earlier year (before the current review period), which was declined by the Cook Islands.
C.3.2 Confidentiality of other information

402. The confidentiality provisions in the Cook Islands' EOI instruments and domestic law do not draw a distinction between information received in response to requests and information forming part of the requests themselves. All other information, such as background documents, communications between the requesting and the requested authorities and within the tax authorities, are treated confidentially.

403. EOI data is treated separately from the rest of the tax data and stored securely in the Collector's office. Requests received from partners are not provided to other RMD staff or information holders when seeking requested information. Templates used by the EOI unit for the purposes of obtaining information from taxpayers, banks and other third parties are consistent with distilling from an exchange partner's request the minimum information necessary to action the request. In general, nothing in the templates or notices sent in practice identifies that the request for information relates to an EOI request, and the access powers quoted are the same as used for domestic purposes. In the exceptional scenario described in paragraph 337 where it is necessary to identify the international agreement that is relevant to the information notice, that minimum information is provided and nothing more.
Confidentiality in practice

404. The Cook Islands' policies and procedures relevant to confidentiality for EOI are a combination of government wide requirements and specific policies and procedures developed by the RMD for internal use.
Human resources

405. The Cook Island's government has centralised human resource management in the Corporate Service Department, which conducts background checks of prospective government employees. In accordance with the Government Recruitment Policy Shortlisted, applicants must declare any criminal convictions or pending criminal court proceedings. Furthermore, the policy requires the recruitment panel to conduct verifications of information provided by the applicant in terms of references, education and previous employment. For contractors, the Contracting for Services Policy requires the RMD to perform due diligence of prospective contractors as a part of the procurement process. The due diligence requires relevant references from previous or current clients. Background checks, including criminal background checks, are conducted in proportion to the nature of the project being contracted out and the risk level.

406. The Corporate Services Department also has oversight responsibility for training governmental employees, including RMD employees. In addition to “on-the-job” continuous training, training material is provided via an online repository and includes subjects related to information security. All staff members receive emails with notification of any changes in policies or security obligations. New employees are subject to an induction training which includes coverage of confidentiality requirements, conflict and general information security requirements. Subsequently, managers are responsible for assessing staff’s knowledge of and adherence to information security requirements as a part of the regular performance reviews and may assign specific training to employees when the need is identified. The EOI unit participates in various events provided by the Global Forum on aspects of information exchange and information security.
Physical and IT security measures

407. Access past the public area of the RMD office is restricted. Visitors that need access to other areas must be registered with the RMD employee responsible for the visit. Visitors sign a visitor log and are required to carry visitor passes. Visitors are escorted at all times. The same applies to building maintenance staff and contractors. There are surveillance cameras strategically placed outside and inside RMD's building with active monitoring during office hours.

408. Access to the dedicated area where the secure perimeter is housed is strictly controlled and only EOI unit staff members have access to it. Entrance to the area is guarded by surveillance cameras and electronic keypads. The Collector's office where EOIR documentation is stored and the office of the Senior Tax Auditor which is a part of the secure perimeter are locked and only the Collector and the Senior Tax Auditor have access to the keys.

409. Access rights to governmental systems and applications, including EOI records, are role based, and access needs are identified during the onboarding process and must be approved by relevant managers. Privileged access rights must be approved by the Collector. The provisioning, change and de-provisioning of accesses are tracked. All access rights are reviewed regularly by the Collector of the RMD and the ICT Division. All users are unique and authenticate themselves with a username and password. Passwords are automatically set to renew every three months and there are adequate requirements for their complexity.
Identification and storage of exchanged information

410. If a partner's information request or a response to a Cook Island's request is paper based, each page is clearly stamped with a message to denote its status under an international agreement and with a warning that its use and disclosure is subject to that agreement. Paper documents are stored in a lockable cabinet located within the secure perimeter, accessible only to the Competent Authority and authorized personnel. For electronic EOI records, a designated locked folder is used specifically for international tax, accessible only to the Competent Authority and EOI unit staff. If not already digitally watermarked by the partner, the Cook Islands adds a watermark to show the treaty status of the document. Upon expiry and when deemed necessary, physical documents are disposed of in accordance with the RMD Disposal of Property Policy – either incinerated or burned under direct supervision by a designated staff member, ensuring complete destruction.

Breach monitoring and response

411. There is a Security Incident and Event Management tool in place where logs are gathered and automatically analysed with built-in use cases that generate alerts based on those definitions. It collects logs from workstations via the Endpoint Detection and Response, from firewalls, web servers, email servers, and office applications. An oath of secrecy is signed by all staff and there is an obligation for them to maintain and report to the Collector any potential breaches of secrecy. All internal and external emails can be monitored at the instruction of the Collector. The ICT Division procures external audit services from consulting companies to cover IT audits, and a complete IT audit (organisational and technical) of the RMD was recently conducted and the secure perimeter was in scope for that audit.

412. In practice, the RMD advises that there have been no instances where information received by the Competent Authority has been improperly disclosed. The Cook Islands' peers have not raised any issues regarding confidentiality during the period of review.
C.4 Rights and safeguards of taxpayers and third parties
The information exchange mechanisms should respect the rights and safeguards of taxpayers and third parties.
413. The standard allows requested parties not to supply information in response to a request in certain identified situations where an issue of trade, business or other legitimate secret arises.

414. Pursuant to all of the Cook Islands' EOI instruments, the contracting parties are not obliged to provide information which would disclose any trade, business, industrial, commercial or professional secret or trade process, or information the disclosure of which would be contrary to public policy. The 2015 Report concluded that the Cook Islands' legal framework and practices concerning rights and safeguards of taxpayers and third parties was in line with the standard.

415. Communication between an attorney or other legal representative and a client are only privileged to the extent that the attorney or other legal representative acts in his or her capacity as an attorney or other legal representative. Where attorney-client privilege is more broadly defined, it does not provide valid grounds on which to decline a request for exchange of information (see also element B.1.5).
416. The EOI instruments of the Cook Islands meet the standard for the protection and rights of taxpayers and third parties.

417. The Cook Islands authorities advised that there have been no practical difficulties experienced in responding to EOI requests due to the application of rights and safeguards in the Cook Islands and peers raised no concerns for the period under review.
418. The conclusions are as follows:
Legal and regulatory framework: In place
No material deficiencies have been identified in the information exchange mechanisms of the Cook Islands in respect of the rights and safeguards of taxpayers and third parties.
Practical implementation of the standard: Compliant
No material deficiencies have been identified in respect of the rights and safeguards of taxpayers and third parties.

C.5 Requesting and providing information in an effective manner
The jurisdiction should request and provide information under its network of agreements in an effective manner.

419. The 2015 Report issued a “Largely Compliant” rating for Element C.5 and did not identify specific issues or legal restrictions on the ability of the Cook Islands’ Competent Authority to provide information in an effective manner. At that time, the volume of requests received was small (five in the review period). While the 2015 Report found that resources and organisational processes for EOI were adequate so far, a recommendation was made that the Cook Islands continue to monitor the practical implementation, particularly in case of any significant changes in volumes of EOI requests.

420. Since 2015, the volume of inward EOI requests to the Cook Islands has scarcely increased (seven in the current review period) and remains relatively low. In the current review period the outward volume was relatively low at six in total, which was in line with volumes in prior years, and is therefore unlikely to have strained the capacity of the assigned resources. As described later in this section, the resources and organisational processes in place are considered to be sufficient for current and foreseeable future volumes of EOI requests. The Cook Islands is now rated Compliant with Element C.5 of the standard.
421. The conclusions are as follows:
Legal and regulatory framework
This element involves issues of practice. Accordingly, no determination has been made.
Practical implementation of the standard: Compliant
No material deficiencies have been identified in exchange of information in practice.
C.5.1 Timeliness of responses to requests for information

422. In order for EOI to be effective, it needs to be provided in a timeframe that allows tax authorities to apply the information to the relevant cases. If a response is provided but only after a significant lapse of time, the information may no longer be of use to the requesting authorities. This is particularly important in the context of international co-operation as cases in this area must be of sufficient importance to warrant making a request.

423. There are no legal restrictions on the ability of the Cook Islands' Competent Authority to respond to requests within 90 days of receipt by providing the information requested or by providing an update on the status of the request.

424. During the review period from 1 April 2022 to 31 March 2025, the Cook Islands received seven requests for information, $^{35}$ coming from four exchange partners. Experience over many years has shown that the main exchange partners are Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, although in the current review period partners included Argentina and Lithuania.

$^{35}$ The Cook Islands counts each request with multiple taxpayers as one request, i.e. if a partner jurisdiction is requesting information about four persons in one request, the Cook Islands counts this as one request. If a further request is made that relates to a previous request, the Cook Islands may count this as a new request but only if it relates to persons not identified in the original request.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: COOK ISLANDS 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

425. Two requests were received in each of the years ending 31 March 2023 and 31 March 2024, and three requests were received in the year ending 31 March 2025. Two requests took slightly longer than 90 days to be responded to, a further three took longer but still within 180 days, and the remaining two were answered within one year. No requests were declined or withdrawn.

426. The information sought in the requests generally related to trusts and persons – individuals or companies – believed to be connected to trusts, with the types of information requested relating to legal ownership and beneficial ownership information (all seven cases), accounting information (all seven cases) and banking information (five cases). Additionally, other types of information were requested in five cases.

427. The information requested is generally not held by the tax administration and so must be obtained from third parties, commonly from banks and the trustee companies. Banks are very responsive and reply quickly. Trustee companies tend to take longer, with the average time to respond to requests in the review period being 28 days. All requests took longer than 90 days to provide a complete response to the partners. The Cook Islands explained that two were only slightly beyond 90 days, one was due to additional efforts by the Cook Islands in seeking records relating to a struck off company even though this was beyond the minimum six-year retention period, and three requests required follow up with the partner to clarify identity information. Reasons have not been provided in one case.

428. These partners were satisfied with the responses and raised no concerns, other than one partner mentioning that it did not receive a status update within 90 days for a request that was actioned between 91 and 180 days of it making the request.
Status updates and communication with partners

429. The standard requires jurisdictions to provide an update on the status of requests when they are unable to respond to a request within 90 days. The provision of status updates is documented in the Cook Islands' EOI manual and electronic calendar reminders are set to ensure these are not missed. Where information is not readily available, the Cook Islands must inform the treaty partner that the information is being sought, within 90 days from receipt of the request.

430. One partner reported not having received a status update. The Cook Islands states that a status update was prepared to be sent to the partner within the required timeframe and in accordance with its procedures, however through an oversight was not sent. This may be a one-off case given that EOI staff demonstrated that they are conversant with the requirements and that procedures are documented, and it is also noted that the full response to the request was sent to the partner soon after the 90 days from the receipt of the original request.
C.5.2 Organisational processes and resources
Organisation of the competent authority

431. The Competent Authority for EOI purposes is the Collector of the RMD, which is a division of the Ministry of Finance and Economic Management. The RMD is the tax and customs collection authority for the Cook Islands. Two additional personnel (out of 35 staff in the RMD in total) are allocated the responsibility for EOI matters (both EOIR and AEOI), being a Tax Examiner and a Senior Tax Auditor, who report directly to the Collector. A third person with several years' experience in EOI and other international tax matters is also available as an advisor. The details of the Competent Authority are identifiable on the tax section of the Ministry of Finance and Economic Management website, and with the Global Forum. Updates as to contact details of the EOI unit are provided to most frequent EOI partners, usually by telephone conferences.
GLOBAL FORUM ON TRANSPARENCY AND EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION FOR TAX PURPOSES: COOK ISLANDS 2026 (SECOND ROUND) © OECD 2026

432. The Collector attends Global Forum meetings as well as EOI training sessions. One of the two EOI staff has attended in person and online workshops hosted by the Global Forum and the Asian Development Bank that have covered EOI, and both EOI staff are engaged in on-the-job training guided by the advisor.
Procedure to handle incoming requests

433. Procedures for handling EOI requests are set out in a step-by-step guide developed by the Collector. Where relevant, the Global Forum model manual on EOI has also been consulted and templates from that manual have been adapted for use when the need has arisen. Staff demonstrated some familiarity with the manual as well as an ability to apply those generic procedures to the Cook Islands appropriately, although as at December 2025 it had not been tailored as a complete Cook Islands specific manual. To ensure full business continuity in case of change of staff, the Cook Islands should complete the necessary adjustments of the model manual to make a Cook Island specific manual (see Annex 1).

434. All EOI requests are sent to, or by, the Collector. The Collector is closely involved in EOI matters, which is facilitated by the direct reporting of EOI staff to her. While the EOI staff carry out the administrative steps in actioning requests in accordance with documented procedures, including checking that documents and information obtained properly responds to a request, the low volumes of requests also allow the Collector to be closely engaged in ensuring the adequacy of information gathered. A spreadsheet-based register is used to track requests, with shared (and restricted) electronic calendars and folders also used by the responsible staff facilitating management of request cases.

435. The 2015 Report concluded that the Cook Islands had committed resources and had in place organisational processes for exchange of information that appeared to be adequate for dealing with incoming EOI requests. Since the Cook Islands had received relatively few requests during that review period, it was recommended to continue to monitor the practical implementation of the organisational processes of the EOI unit, in particular taking account of any significant changes to the volume of incoming EOI requests, to ensure that they are sufficient for effective EOI in practice. Since 2015, the volume of inward EOI requests to the Cook Islands has not materially increased (seven in the current review period) so remains relatively low in absolute terms. The number of outward requests during the current review period was also relatively low at six in total. This is despite the scope of exchange partners covered by exchange agreements substantially increasing due to the Cook Islands becoming a party to the Multilateral Convention. As the volumes have been relatively stable over the long term, the resources and organisational processes in place are considered to be sufficient for current and foreseeable future volumes of EOI requests. $^{36}$
Outgoing requests

436. The 2016 Terms of Reference includes an additional requirement to ensure the quality of requests made by assessed jurisdictions. Over the review period, the Cook Islands made six outbound EOI requests, three of which were group requests. No requests for clarification were made by the relevant partners. Outbound requests are coordinated through the EOI unit, with documented procedures included in the EOI manual, and a template is used by both the tax auditor wishing to make the request and the EOI staff that evaluate the appropriateness of the request before sending it.

437. One outward request may not have been fully appropriate in the circumstances or at least may have been prematurely made before all reasonable domestic measures had been pursued, see also paragraph 353. This request related to information that had been formally requested from a Cook Islands taxpayer, for which the taxpayer had failed to cooperate. Under the Income Tax Act, the Cook Islands could have taken steps to seek assistance from the High Court to obtain the requested information. However, the RMD opted not to escalate action through these domestic judicial procedures, instead it only sought such information from an exchange partner whose taxpayer was a contractual counterparty with, and a related party of, the Cook Islands taxpayer. Under the standard, a jurisdiction should generally take all reasonable measures to obtain information domestically before seeking it from an exchange partner. Whether or not those domestic measures could have been disproportionately difficult is not known as they have never been used. However, the Cook Islands authority assures that it is an isolated case caused by staff unfamiliar with the requirements at the time. The EOI Manual has since been updated with instructions for staff on measures to be taken before making a request of an exchange partner. The Cook Islands should ensure that it only makes requests for information from partners when it has taken all reasonable steps to obtain that information domestically (see Annex 1).

$^{36}$ Additional evidence that the volumes of requests have remained low and relatively stable over the long term is that in the three-year period ending 31 March 2021, nine requests were received by the Cook Islands, and it sent three requests.

\- The Cook Islands should clarify in guidance the operation of the definition of beneficial owner in relation to professional advisors and managers (paragraphs 134 and 149).
\- The Cook Islands should ensure that ownership information is available in the event that bearer shares are issued (paragraph 162).

Identity information on partners in domestic partnerships is required to be available under tax law, however there is a very narrow circumstance where this might not be the case if all partners are entities or legal arrangements. The Cook Islands should ensure that all domestic partnerships relevant under the standard are identifiable through tax registrations and/or through the filing of tax returns (paragraph 176).

The Cook Islands should ensure that any approvals to retain accounting records for less than seven completed accounting periods does not interfere with the availability of accounting information as required by the standard (see paragraph 251).

text: Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters (as amended)

The Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters was developed jointly by the OECD and the Council of Europe in 1988 and amended in 2010 (the Multilateral Convention). $^{37}$ The Multilateral Convention is the most comprehensive multilateral instrument available for all forms of tax cooperation to tackle tax evasion and avoidance, a top priority for all jurisdictions.

The original 1988 Convention was amended to respond to the call of the G20 at its April 2009 London Summit to align it to the standard on exchange of information on request and to open it to all countries, in particular to ensure that developing countries could benefit from the new more transparent environment. The Multilateral Convention was opened for signature on 1 June 2011.

The Multilateral Convention was signed by the Cook Islands on 28 October 2016 and entered into force on 1 September 2017. The Cook Islands can exchange information with all other Parties to the Multilateral Convention.

$^{37}$ The amendments to the 1988 Convention were embodied into two separate instruments achieving the same purpose: the amended Convention (the Multilateral Convention) which integrates the amendments into a consolidated text, and the Protocol amending the 1988 Convention which sets out the amendments separately.

Annex 3. Methodology for the review

The Cook Islands underwent a combined review (Phase 1 and Phase 2) of its legal and regulatory framework and the implementation of the framework in practice in 2015. The 2015 Review was conducted according to the terms of reference approved by the Global Forum in February 2010 and the Methodology used in the first round of reviews.

This second-round peer review is based on the 2016 Terms of Reference and has been conducted in accordance with the 2016 Methodology for peer reviews and non-member reviews, as approved by the Global Forum in October 2015 and amended in 2020 and 2021, and the Schedule of Reviews.

The Round 2 review of the Cook Islands was launched in September 2021. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the onsite visit that was scheduled to take place in December 2021 could not take place. Consequently, the review of the Cook Islands has been conducted in two phases, with a desk-based Phase 1 review leading to the adoption in August 2022 of the report assessing the legal and regulatory framework of the Cook Islands against the 2016 Terms of Reference (Phase 1 report). The subsequent scheduling of the Phase 2 review with an onsite visit then took account of the limited experience of the Cook Islands in exchange of information, with the visit ultimately taking place in November 2025. The present review complements the first report with an assessment of the practical implementation of the standard, including in respect of exchange of information requests received and sent during the review period from 1 April 2022 to 31 March 2025. Changes made to the legal framework since the Phase 1 review as at 6 May 2022 have also been assessed.

The evaluation is based on information available to the assessment team including the exchange of information arrangements signed, laws and regulations in force or effective as at 7 May 2026, Cook Islands' responses to the EOIR questionnaire, inputs from partner jurisdictions, as well as information provided by the Cook Islands' authorities during the on-site visit that took place from 24 to 26 November 2025 in Avarua, Cook Islands. As the Cook Islands has limited experience in exchange of information on request, the review of this jurisdiction was conducted in two phases, in accordance with the new section V of the Methodology, as amended in 2021. Peer Review on Transparency and Exchange of Information on Request COOK ISLANDS 2026 (Second Round)
The Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes is a multilateral framework within which over 170 jurisdictions participate on an equal footing.

The Global Forum monitors and peer reviews the implementation of the international standards on transparency and exchange of information on request (EOIR) and on automatic exchange of information. The EOIR provides for international exchange on request of information foreseeably relevant to the administration or enforcement of the tax laws of a requesting party. All Global Forum members have agreed to have their implementation of the EOIR standard assessed by peer review. In addition, non-members that are relevant to the Global Forum's work are also subject to review. The legal and regulatory framework of each jurisdiction is assessed, as is the implementation of that framework in practice. The final result is an overall rating of the compliance of the jurisdiction with the standard.

The first round of reviews was conducted from 2010 to 2016. A second round of reviews started in 2016. Peer reviews are generally conducted in one go, but they can be conducted in two separate reviews, with a Phase 1 reviewing the legal framework, followed by a Phase 2 focussing on practice. Reviews are phased when jurisdictions have limited EOIR experience or in exceptional circumstances, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The review reports are published and assessed jurisdictions are expected to follow up on any recommendations made. The ultimate goal is to help jurisdictions to effectively implement the standard of transparency and exchange of information on request for tax purposes.

This peer review report analyses the practical implementation of the standard on transparency and exchange of information on request (EOIR) for the Cook Islands, as part of the second round of reviews conducted by the Global Forum since 2016.
